one_line: SAM point prompts carry a hidden distance-to-boundary prior: mask topology changes systematically with where inside the object you click
problem: Interactive SAM results vary wildly between users clicking the same object, and nobody can predict which clicks fail; the click position inside the object is treated as irrelevant noise.
core_hypothesis: SA-1B interactive annotation sampled clicks non-uniformly (biased toward region centers), so SAM learned an implicit prior mapping normalized medial-axis distance of the click to expected mask granularity; clicks near boundaries systematically select thinner sub-parts.
falsifiable_prediction: For a fixed object and fixed image, IoU and selected-mask granularity will vary as a smooth monotone function of the click's distance-transform value, and the effect size will be larger for objects with part structure than for blobs.
why_important: If click position is a controllable latent variable, prompt placement policies (not model tuning) can recover a large fraction of interactive performance for free in every deployment.
why_possibly_novel: SAM prompt studies typically report robustness to random jitter; a stratified analysis by medial-axis distance treating placement as a structured prior rather than noise appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take ~200 objects from any segmentation dataset with GT masks, compute distance transforms, sample 20 clicks per object stratified by normalized medial-axis distance, run frozen SAM, regress IoU and mask-area rank against the distance stratum.
main_risk: The effect may be confounded by local appearance (boundary pixels are also low-contrast), making the prior appear geometric when it is photometric.
default_community_belief: Click position within the object is unstructured noise; robustness to jitter is the only property worth measuring.
why_it_might_be_wrong: SAM's prompt encoder uses only positional encodings of the click; granularity selection may be handled entirely by the multimask heads independent of click geometry.
fastest_falsification: One afternoon: 50 objects, 10 stratified clicks each, plot IoU vs distance stratum; a flat curve kills the idea.

one_line: Box prompts act as hard spatial gates, not soft priors: SAM almost never segments beyond the box even when the object visibly continues
problem: Practitioners assume a slightly-too-small box is a benign under-specification, but truncated boxes may cause guaranteed truncated masks, which matters for detector-cascade pipelines feeding imperfect boxes to SAM.
core_hypothesis: The box corner embeddings induce an effectively hard crop in decoder cross-attention, so mask probability outside the box is suppressed multiplicatively rather than being re-estimated from image evidence.
falsifiable_prediction: Mask recall outside the box boundary will be near zero even when 30% of the object extends beyond it, while the same region is segmented perfectly when the box is enlarged; the failure will be asymmetric (over-large boxes are cheap, under-sized boxes are catastrophic).
why_important: Every detection-then-segment pipeline inherits this asymmetry; a one-line fix (systematic box dilation calibrated per domain) could beat expensive fine-tuning for truncation errors.
why_possibly_novel: Box-quality sensitivity studies exist informally, but framing the box as a hard gate with an asymmetric loss landscape, and calibrating optimal dilation per domain as a 1-parameter adaptation, appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On any instance dataset, shrink GT boxes by 5-30% on one side, measure recall of mask pixels outside the shrunk box vs a control with correct boxes; then sweep a global dilation factor and measure the trade-off curve.
main_risk: SAM may behave softly for small truncations and only gate hard for large ones, making the finding a rediscovery of obvious sensitivity rather than a structural claim.
default_community_belief: Boxes are robust prompts and small box errors cause proportionally small mask errors.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The decoder attends globally to image tokens, so evidence outside the box is available and may win when contrast is strong; the gating may be a soft prior after all.
fastest_falsification: 100 images with one-side-shrunk boxes, measure outside-box mask recall; if recall degrades gracefully and symmetrically, the hard-gate claim dies.

one_line: Negative clicks are undertrained relative to positive clicks: an information-matched negative click helps far less than a positive one
problem: Interactive pipelines treat positive and negative clicks as symmetric information sources, but if SAM processes them asymmetrically, correction strategies built on negative clicks silently waste user effort.
core_hypothesis: SA-1B's interactive stage generated far fewer negative-click events than positive ones, so the learned negative-point embedding occupies a poorly-shaped region of prompt space and produces weaker, less spatially precise suppression.
falsifiable_prediction: In matched-pair trials where a positive click on a missed region and a negative click on a false-positive region carry equal corrective information (equal error area), the positive click will recover systematically more IoU, and the gap will widen out-of-domain.
why_important: If confirmed, interactive UIs and click-simulation training schedules should be redesigned around positive-first strategies, and PEFT of only the negative-point embedding (a few hundred parameters) becomes a targeted, near-free fix.
why_possibly_novel: Click-type asymmetry is folklore among practitioners but an information-matched quantification and a parameter-isolated fix (retune one embedding vector) do not appear to exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct paired correction scenarios on ~300 images where error regions for FP and FN have equal area and similar contrast; apply one corrective click of each type; compare IoU recovery distributions.
main_risk: Equalizing 'information content' of clicks is hard; area-matched errors may not be difficulty-matched, and the asymmetry could reflect task geometry rather than training imbalance.
default_community_belief: Positive and negative clicks are symmetric correction tools; more clicks of either type monotonically improve masks.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Suppression may be inherently easier than discovery for a decoder, so the asymmetry might be architectural and unfixable by retuning the embedding.
fastest_falsification: Retune only the negative-point embedding on a small correction dataset; if the asymmetry persists exactly, the undertraining explanation is falsified.

one_line: Interactive SAM is path-dependent: the same final set of clicks yields different masks depending on click order
problem: Evaluation protocols and training simulators assume the final prompt set determines the mask, but iterative prompting feeds previous mask logits back as dense prompts, creating hysteresis nobody measures.
core_hypothesis: The dense-prompt feedback loop makes interactive SAM a dynamical system with multiple attractors; click order selects the attractor, and out-of-domain images have more attractors (higher path sensitivity).
falsifiable_prediction: Permuting the order of an identical 4-click set will change final IoU by a measurable margin on a nontrivial fraction of images, and this path-sensitivity rate will correlate with domain gap better than single-click IoU does.
why_important: Path dependence breaks the equivalence between simulated and human evaluation, and offers a free unsupervised domain-shift meter for deciding when adaptation is needed.
why_possibly_novel: Interactive segmentation papers report clicks-to-target curves but treat the click sequence as exchangeable; a hysteresis analysis of SAM's feedback loop appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For 200 images, fix 4 corrective clicks derived from GT errors, run all 24 orderings, report the distribution of final-IoU ranges per image, in-domain vs out-of-domain.
main_risk: Path sensitivity may exist but be dominated by the first click only, collapsing the finding into 'first click matters', which is already known.
default_community_belief: The final prompt set determines the output; click order is an implementation detail.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If implementations re-run the decoder from scratch with the full prompt set each step and discard logit feedback, the system is order-invariant by construction.
fastest_falsification: 20 images, all orderings of 3 clicks with logit feedback enabled; if final masks are pixel-identical across orders, the idea dies immediately.

one_line: Prompt-token activations occupy a tiny linear subspace; tuning only that subspace ('prompt-subspace PEFT') could match LoRA at 1/1000 the parameters
problem: PEFT for SAM is spent on encoder weights, but if the interface between prompts and decoder is intrinsically low-dimensional, the cheapest adaptation lever is being ignored.
core_hypothesis: Across natural prompts, prompt-token embeddings concentrate in a subspace of dimension <=8; domain adaptation mostly requires re-orienting this subspace, not changing image features.
falsifiable_prediction: PCA of prompt-token embeddings will show >95% variance in <=8 of 256 dimensions, and training only an 8x8 rotation plus bias on that subspace will recover >=70% of the gain of decoder-LoRA on at least half of tested domain shifts.
why_important: A parameter budget of a few hundred floats enables per-user, per-scanner, even per-session adaptation with no infrastructure, and cleanly separates 'prompt interpretation gap' from 'feature gap'.
why_possibly_novel: PEFT work targets weights of attention/FFN layers; treating the measured empirical subspace of prompt activations as the adaptation surface is a different object than prefix tuning (which adds tokens rather than reshaping the existing interface).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect prompt-token embeddings over 10k prompts, do PCA; then freeze everything, train the low-dim affine map on one adaptation task, compare to decoder-LoRA at matched wall-clock.
main_risk: The subspace may be low-dimensional only because prompt types are few; within-subspace tuning may be expressively too weak for real gaps.
default_community_belief: Meaningful adaptation requires touching backbone or decoder weights; the prompt interface is too small to matter.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Domain gaps that are genuinely feature-level (new textures, new physics) cannot be fixed by re-mapping prompts no matter how the subspace is rotated.
fastest_falsification: The PCA alone is a one-hour experiment; if prompt embeddings are full-rank across prompts, the premise collapses.

one_line: Most of SAM's domain gap may be prompt-interpretation gap: a tiny learned click-remapping MLP (image-conditioned virtual clicks) recovers it without touching the backbone
problem: When SAM fails on a new domain, the community reflexively adapts features, but the failure may be that the model misreads what the click means in that domain (e.g., click on organ selects tissue class).
core_hypothesis: For a large class of domain shifts, there exists a small displacement-and-reweighting function of the user click (conditioned on local embedding statistics) that makes frozen SAM behave as if fine-tuned; the gap is in prompt semantics, not features.
falsifiable_prediction: A 2-layer MLP (<50k params) mapping (click position, local feature patch) to a set of virtual clicks will close >=50% of the zero-shot-to-fine-tuned IoU gap on at least some standard domain-shifted benchmarks, while pure decoder-LoRA of equal parameter count closes less.
why_important: It changes the diagnosis of foundation-model transfer failure: if prompt reinterpretation suffices, adaptation becomes deployable on frozen, shared, cached backbones (no per-domain model copies).
why_possibly_novel: Prompt engineering for SAM exists as hand-crafted heuristics; learning an image-conditioned click transformation as the sole trainable component, and using it to decompose domain gap into prompt-gap vs feature-gap, appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pick 3 domain-shifted datasets; train the click-remapper with frozen SAM vs decoder-LoRA at matched parameters and data; report gap closure fractions and cross-domain decomposition.
main_risk: Virtual-click search may just exploit the multimask head (equivalent to oracle mask selection), inflating apparent gains.
default_community_belief: Domain gaps live in the image encoder; prompts are a thin deterministic interface not worth learning.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Severe modality shifts change the features themselves, and no click remapping can conjure discriminative features that are absent.
fastest_falsification: Oracle experiment first: grid-search virtual click positions per image with GT; if even oracle virtual clicks cannot close the gap, the learned version cannot either — one GPU-day.

one_line: SAM degrades beyond a critical number of point prompts because SA-1B interactive training rarely exceeded a few clicks per mask
problem: Power users add many clicks to fix hard cases, assuming monotone improvement, but heavily-prompted SAM may leave its training distribution and produce worse masks than with fewer clicks.
core_hypothesis: There is a click-count threshold (est. 6-9) beyond which marginal clicks have negative expected value out-of-domain, because prompt-token attention patterns were never trained at that density.
falsifiable_prediction: Clicks-to-IoU curves will be non-monotone on a measurable fraction of hard images, with the peak-then-decline pattern appearing earlier out-of-domain than in-domain.
why_important: Interactive tools should implement click budgets or prompt consolidation; PEFT recipes should include high-click-count simulation, a data dimension nobody controls today.
why_possibly_novel: Clicks-to-target curves are always reported as averages, hiding per-image non-monotonicity; a distributional analysis of marginal click value at high counts appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On 300 hard images (zero-shot IoU<0.6), simulate up to 15 corrective clicks with a fixed policy, record per-image IoU trajectories, count non-monotone trajectories and locate peak positions.
main_risk: Non-monotonicity may be an artifact of the click simulator rather than the model; requires cross-checking with two different simulation policies.
default_community_belief: More corrective clicks never hurt; curves saturate but do not decline.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The decoder may treat prompt tokens near-independently so density does not matter, and reported saturation is genuine saturation.
fastest_falsification: 50 hard images, 15 simulated clicks each, plot per-image trajectories; absence of decline falsifies within hours.

one_line: Extreme aspect-ratio boxes (>20:1) fall outside SAM's prompt statistics and cause systematic under-segmentation of thin elongated structures
problem: Thin structures (cracks, wires, vessels, seams) are a known SAM weakness, universally blamed on encoder resolution, but part of the failure may be that the box prompt itself is out-of-distribution.
core_hypothesis: The positional-encoding representation of box corners was trained on SA-1B box statistics with bounded aspect ratios; extreme boxes produce corner-embedding pairs the decoder never saw, causing prompt-side failure that is separable from feature-side failure.
falsifiable_prediction: For synthetic elongated objects rendered at controlled aspect ratios on fixed backgrounds, IoU will drop sharply beyond a critical aspect ratio even when per-pixel contrast is held constant, and replacing one extreme box by several square sub-boxes will partially restore IoU without any weight change.
why_important: It isolates a fixable prompt-representation failure inside a famous failure mode, and yields an immediate training-free mitigation (box tiling) plus a targeted PEFT (retrain corner embeddings on synthetic extreme boxes).
why_possibly_novel: Thin-structure failures are always attributed to patch resolution; an ablation separating prompt-OOD from feature-OOD via sub-box decomposition appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Synthetic benchmark: bars at aspect ratios 2:1 to 100:1 with matched contrast; compare full-box vs tiled-sub-box prompting on frozen SAM; if tiling helps substantially, prompt-OOD is confirmed as a separable cause.
main_risk: Feature-level resolution loss may dominate so completely that the prompt effect, though real, is practically irrelevant.
default_community_belief: Thin-structure failure is purely an encoder resolution problem; the prompt representation is aspect-ratio-agnostic by construction.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Fourier positional encodings may extrapolate smoothly to extreme corner configurations, leaving nothing prompt-side to fix.
fastest_falsification: Render 100 synthetic bars, sweep aspect ratio, compare box vs tiled prompting — a few GPU-hours.

one_line: The dense mask-prompt pathway is nearly a no-op for out-of-domain inputs: an ablation audit of SAM's least-understood input channel
problem: Many adaptation pipelines feed coarse masks (from heuristics or previous models) into SAM's dense prompt input assuming it strongly conditions the output, but its causal contribution has never been isolated.
core_hypothesis: The dense-prompt convolutions learned to encode only self-generated logit patterns from SA-1B's interactive loop; externally supplied masks (different statistics: binary, smoothed, or eroded) are largely ignored or misread by the decoder.
falsifiable_prediction: Feeding GT masks as dense prompts will improve output IoU only marginally over no dense prompt, while feeding SAM's own previous logits will change outputs substantially; the discrepancy will be larger for binary external masks than for logit-like ones.
why_important: Pipelines that inject priors via the mask channel (weak-label bootstrapping, cascade refinement) may be building on a dead input; knowing this redirects engineering effort to prompt or logit-space injection.
why_possibly_novel: The dense-prompt channel's sensitivity to input statistics (binary vs logit-shaped) is undocumented; the community treats it as a generic mask input.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On 200 images, run SAM with (a) no dense prompt, (b) GT binary mask, (c) GT mask converted to logit-like soft values matching SAM's own logit histogram, (d) SAM's own previous-iteration logits; compare output deltas.
main_risk: Results may depend heavily on the click prompts co-supplied, requiring a careful factorial design to avoid confounding.
default_community_belief: The dense mask prompt is a strong conditioning signal usable for injecting external priors.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The convolutions may generalize fine across mask statistics, and observed pipeline failures may have other causes.
fastest_falsification: The 4-condition ablation on 50 images runs in under an hour and immediately reveals whether external binary masks move outputs.

one_line: Prompt-jitter robustness radius is a better unsupervised domain-gap meter than IoU-head confidence, telling you where PEFT is needed without labels
problem: Teams must decide which deployment domains need adaptation before collecting labels, but the standard signal (SAM's own IoU prediction) is itself miscalibrated under domain shift, creating circular reasoning.
core_hypothesis: The radius of prompt perturbation under which SAM's output mask stays stable is a behavioral invariant that degrades monotonically with true domain gap, and unlike the IoU head it does not rely on a possibly-shifted learned calibration.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a suite of domains with known fine-tuning gains, mean jitter-stability radius (max click displacement keeping mask IoU-to-itself >0.9) will rank domains by true zero-shot deficit with higher rank correlation than mean IoU-head score.
why_important: A label-free, model-internal triage metric decides where to spend annotation and PEFT budget; this is the missing 'when to adapt' tool while all research focuses on 'how to adapt'.
why_possibly_novel: Stability under prompt perturbation is computed in SAM's automatic mask generator as a mask-quality filter, but its aggregate use as a domain-level shift detector benchmarked against confidence appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Choose 6 datasets with published or self-computed fine-tuned vs zero-shot gaps; compute mean stability radius and mean IoU-head score per dataset on 200 unlabeled images each; compare Spearman correlations with the true gap.
main_risk: Stability radius may saturate (fully stable or fully unstable) across realistic domains, giving poor resolution exactly where decisions are hard.
default_community_belief: Model confidence (the IoU head) is the natural signal for detecting domain shift in SAM.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Some domains may be unstable to jitter for benign reasons (many valid granularities), decoupling instability from true error.
fastest_falsification: Two domains with known large/small gaps, 100 images each; if the radius fails to separate them but IoU-head does, the claim is dead in a day.

one_line: SAM's three multimask tokens have stable whole/part/subpart roles across domains, enabling granularity routing by tuning only one token embedding
problem: Adaptation to tasks with a fixed target granularity (always the whole organ, always the sub-part) retrains large parts of the model to do what may be a token-selection problem.
core_hypothesis: Each multimask output token encodes a granularity role that is approximately domain-invariant; matching the task's granularity to the right token and tuning only that token's embedding (256 floats) captures most of the adaptation gain for granularity-mismatch failures.
falsifiable_prediction: Across >=5 domains, the per-token granularity ordering (mean mask area rank) will be conserved, and single-token-embedding tuning will beat full decoder LoRA on tasks whose zero-shot failures are granularity mismatches, while losing on tasks with true boundary failures.
why_important: It splits 'SAM fails on my data' into granularity-mismatch (fixable with 256 parameters) vs representation failure (needs real PEFT), preventing wasted fine-tuning.
why_possibly_novel: Multimask outputs are treated as an ambiguity workaround with an argmax; the token-role-stability claim and token-level PEFT as a diagnostic-driven method appear unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute mask-area rank statistics per token across domains to test role stability; then on 2 granularity-mismatch tasks, compare single-token tuning vs decoder LoRA at matched data.
main_risk: Token roles may be context-dependent (role switching per image), destroying the routing premise.
default_community_belief: Multimask outputs are an inference-time ambiguity hack; adaptation means changing weights, not choosing tokens.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Published SAM analyses show the IoU head already selects appropriate granularity often; remaining failures may rarely be pure granularity mismatch.
fastest_falsification: Token-role stability statistics across 3 domains is a few GPU-hours; unstable roles kill the routing idea before any training.

one_line: SAM's IoU-head miscalibration under domain shift is directional and fixable with a 2-parameter per-domain temperature, giving a free TTA loss
problem: The IoU prediction head is used everywhere (mask selection, filtering, pseudo-labeling) but its error structure under domain shift is unknown, so downstream systems inherit invisible bias.
core_hypothesis: Miscalibration is not random: the head is overconfident on low-texture regions and underconfident on high-frequency clutter, because SA-1B's difficulty-confidence correlation differs from OOD domains; a per-domain affine correction (2 params) restores rank fidelity.
falsifiable_prediction: Binned calibration curves out-of-domain will show a consistent texture-dependent sign pattern across multiple domains, and fitting scale+shift on 50 labeled masks will cut expected calibration error by more than half without touching ranking within texture bins.
why_important: Every SAM-based auto-labeling and active-learning loop keys on this scalar; a 2-parameter fix is the cheapest possible adaptation with system-wide effects.
why_possibly_novel: Calibration of segmentation quality heads (as opposed to classifiers) under domain shift, and the texture-conditional structure of the error, appears unstudied for promptable models.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On 3 OOD datasets, compute predicted-vs-true IoU scatter stratified by local frequency energy of the region; test for the predicted sign pattern; fit affine correction on a 50-mask subset and evaluate ECE on the rest.
main_risk: Miscalibration may be idiosyncratic per domain with no shared structure, making the directional claim false even if correction still works.
default_community_belief: The IoU head roughly transfers; people use its raw scores OOD without correction.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The head conditions on decoder state, not raw texture, so its errors may track decoder uncertainty rather than image frequency content.
fastest_falsification: Predicted-vs-true IoU scatter on one OOD dataset stratified by texture energy: one evening of compute.

one_line: PEFT silently destroys IoU-head calibration even while improving masks: an unmeasured forgetting mode inside the decoder
problem: Papers report mask mIoU after adaptation but never re-validate the quality-prediction head; deployed systems keep using its scores as if calibration survived fine-tuning.
core_hypothesis: Mask-loss gradients flowing through shared decoder trunk hijack features the IoU head depends on; calibration degrades roughly in proportion to adaptation gain unless the head is co-trained or detached.
falsifiable_prediction: Across standard PEFT recipes (LoRA on encoder, decoder tuning, adapter variants), post-adaptation expected calibration error of the IoU head will increase significantly in the majority of runs, and the increase will correlate positively with mask-IoU improvement.
why_important: Auto-selection among multimask outputs, pseudo-label filtering, and human-in-the-loop triage all silently break after PEFT; making calibration a first-class reported metric would change adaptation practice.
why_possibly_novel: Forgetting research measures zero-shot mask quality; forgetting of the auxiliary quality-estimation function is a distinct, unmeasured axis.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take 3 public SAM-PEFT recipes, retrain on one dataset each, measure IoU-head ECE and selection accuracy (does argmax token match best mask) before/after.
main_risk: Some recipes co-train the IoU loss by default, which would mask the effect and require careful recipe stratification.
default_community_belief: If masks improve, the model improved; auxiliary heads are assumed to come along for the ride.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The IoU head may read late-stage mask logits that remain in-distribution after PEFT, leaving calibration intact.
fastest_falsification: One PEFT run with before/after ECE measurement — a single GPU-day.

one_line: Prompt attention collapse: with many prompts, decoder cross-attention mass concentrates on 1-2 prompt tokens, explaining diminishing returns of extra clicks
problem: Extra clicks often do nothing, and nobody knows whether the information is ignored at the attention level or absorbed but overruled.
core_hypothesis: Softmax attention over prompt tokens exhibits winner-take-most dynamics as token count grows; later clicks receive vanishing attention weight, so their information never reaches mask tokens regardless of relevance.
falsifiable_prediction: Measured attention mass on the k-th added click will decay faster than 1/k, and images where extra clicks fail will show significantly higher prompt-attention concentration (Gini coefficient) than images where clicks help.
why_important: If collapse is the bottleneck, the fix is a temperature or normalization change in one attention layer (tunable with a handful of parameters), not more training data — a surgical, mechanism-level PEFT target.
why_possibly_novel: Attention analysis on SAM has focused on the image encoder; prompt-token attention dynamics in the two-way decoder as the mediator of interactive failure appears unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument decoder cross-attention, run 1-10 click sequences on 200 images, correlate per-click attention mass with per-click IoU gain; then tune only the prompt-attention temperature and re-measure.
main_risk: Attention weights are known to be an unreliable proxy for information flow; a gradient-based attribution may be needed to make the causal claim stick.
default_community_belief: Diminishing click returns reflect saturated information in the image, not an architectural bottleneck.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The two-way decoder alternates directions and may redistribute attention in later layers, invalidating single-layer concentration measurements.
fastest_falsification: Attention instrumentation plus temperature-sweep at inference (no training) on 50 images: if higher temperature never helps many-click cases, the collapse story weakens fast.

one_line: The 4x upscaling head, not the encoder, creates most boundary error under domain shift — probe the 256x256 logits before blaming features
problem: Boundary quality drives adaptation demand, and the community assumes coarse boundaries mean the encoder lost detail; but SAM's output path itself (low-res logits then learned upsampling) is a candidate culprit that is never isolated.
core_hypothesis: The transposed-convolution upscaling learned SA-1B boundary statistics (smooth, closed, photographic); under domain shift its learned deblurring prior mismatches true boundary statistics, adding error on top of whatever the encoder lost.
falsifiable_prediction: Boundary-F measured at the internal low-resolution logits (upsampled bilinearly for fairness) will show a smaller in-domain-to-OOD degradation than boundary-F at the final output, implying the learned upscaler amplifies domain gap; retraining only the upscaling head will recover a disproportionate share of boundary metrics.
why_important: If true, the cheapest boundary fix is a tiny head retrain reusing cached embeddings (no encoder passes), changing the default PEFT recipe for boundary-critical domains.
why_possibly_novel: High-quality-mask variants add new modules; a causal attribution study between encoder features and the existing upscaling path, using internal-logit probing, appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On 3 OOD datasets, extract pre-upsample logits, compare boundary-F(internal, bilinear-upsampled) vs boundary-F(final) against in-domain baselines; then retrain only the upscaler on 100 labels per domain.
main_risk: Internal logits at 256x256 may be too coarse for meaningful boundary-F, making the comparison noisy for thin objects.
default_community_belief: Boundary failures under domain shift are encoder-feature failures; the output head is a neutral decoder of whatever the features contain.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The upscaler is small and mostly interpolative; its learned prior may be too weak to carry measurable domain bias.
fastest_falsification: Internal-vs-final boundary-F comparison on one OOD dataset — hours, no training.

one_line: Tune only the hypernetwork MLP that turns mask tokens into dynamic filters: possibly the highest-leverage 3-layer module in SAM
problem: PEFT placement debates cover encoder blocks and attention projections while ignoring that the final mask is literally produced by dynamic filters generated from mask tokens by a tiny MLP.
core_hypothesis: Domain adaptation changes required output filter shapes more than it changes required features; the token-to-filter MLP is where that transformation is concentrated, so tuning it alone captures a disproportionate share of decoder-side adaptation.
falsifiable_prediction: Tuning only the hypernetwork MLP will match or beat LoRA-on-decoder-attention at less than a tenth of the trainable parameters on the majority of tested domain shifts, and its gains will correlate with output-statistic shifts (mask size, boundary curvature) rather than semantic shifts.
why_important: A reliable ultra-cheap tuning site enables per-task adapter storage measured in kilobytes and instant task switching in multi-tenant serving.
why_possibly_novel: The hypernetwork path is architecturally distinctive to SAM-style decoders and absent from standard PEFT placement studies inherited from NLP.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On 4 adaptation tasks, train (a) hypernetwork-MLP-only, (b) decoder-attention LoRA, (c) both, at matched data; compare IoU and parameter counts; analyze which shift types favor (a).
main_risk: The MLP output space is tiny (per-token filters), possibly saturating quickly and capping achievable gains on hard shifts.
default_community_belief: PEFT placement follows NLP conventions: attention projections and FFNs are the levers that matter.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If domain shift mostly corrupts image features, changing the filter generator merely re-decodes corrupted features and gains little.
fastest_falsification: One task, hypernetwork-only vs decoder-LoRA, one GPU-day; a clear loss for (a) at equal data ends the strong version.

one_line: Task arithmetic on mask-token embeddings: tuned token deltas for different shifts (thin-structure, low-contrast) compose additively
problem: Every new domain currently needs its own adaptation run; if small learned deltas compose, a library of primitive corrections could cover the product space of domain factors without training on combinations.
core_hypothesis: Mask-token embedding space is locally linear with respect to interpretable output properties; embedding deltas learned separately for distinct shift factors add with limited interference when factors are approximately orthogonal in effect.
falsifiable_prediction: delta(thin)+delta(low-contrast) applied jointly will recover >=70% of the IoU gain of a jointly-trained delta on data exhibiting both factors, while randomly-paired deltas will show near-zero or negative composition gain.
why_important: Compositional adaptation is the difference between O(k) and O(2^k) training cost over k domain factors, and token-level deltas are cheap enough to ship as a public library.
why_possibly_novel: Task arithmetic is established for full weight deltas in classifiers and LLMs; applying it to 256-float token embeddings of a promptable segmenter, with factor-controlled evaluation, is a different regime and granularity.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct controlled datasets varying two factors independently and jointly; train single-factor token deltas; evaluate additive composition vs joint training on the both-factors split.
main_risk: Factors interact in real images (thin AND low-contrast structures differ qualitatively from either alone), breaking additivity precisely where composition is most needed.
default_community_belief: Meaningful adaptation deltas live in weight space; embedding-level edits are too weak to encode task corrections.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Token embeddings pass through shared nonlinear decoding, so linear composition at the input of that map has no guarantee of linear effects at the output.
fastest_falsification: Two synthetic factors, three training runs, one composition evaluation: roughly two GPU-days.

one_line: SAM's 2-layer decoder is the topology bottleneck: iterating the decoder with tied weights at inference (zero training) improves multi-component and holed masks
problem: SAM struggles with objects that have holes or many components, universally attributed to data or encoder limits, but two rounds of cross-attention may simply be too few message-passing steps to resolve complex topology.
core_hypothesis: Mask topology errors are an iteration-depth deficit: applying the same decoder layers additional times (weight-tied unrolling with logit feedback) provides the missing refinement steps, exposing that depth, not knowledge, is the constraint.
falsifiable_prediction: On a topology-stratified evaluation, weight-tied decoder iteration will improve masks for high-genus and multi-component objects by a measurable margin while leaving simple-blob performance unchanged, with gains saturating after 2-3 extra iterations.
why_important: A training-free inference knob that fixes a structural failure class would be immediately deployable everywhere SAM runs, and it would redirect adaptation research from data to compute allocation.
why_possibly_novel: Recurrent unrolling is standard in some segmentation lineages, but as a zero-training diagnostic separating knowledge-limits from depth-limits in a promptable foundation decoder it appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a topology-stratified subset from existing datasets (genus>=1, components>=3); run SAM with 1-4 tied decoder iterations feeding logits back as dense prompts; compare stratified metrics.
main_risk: The decoder was never trained to consume its own outputs repeatedly at inference-time distribution, so iteration may diverge rather than refine.
default_community_belief: Topology failures need better training data or higher-capacity decoders, i.e. retraining.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The mask-selection and dense-prompt loop already approximates iteration; if so extra unrolling adds nothing beyond existing iterative prompting.
fastest_falsification: 50 holed/multi-component objects, 3 iteration depths, no training: an afternoon.

one_line: SAM has an architectural prior against empty masks, making it structurally unable to say 'nothing here' — and PEFT with empty-mask supervision degrades it disproportionately
problem: Real pipelines feed SAM prompts that sometimes point at nothing (bad detections, user error); SAM always returns some mask, and adaptation attempts that add empty-mask training reportedly destabilize it — a phenomenon without a documented mechanism.
core_hypothesis: The dynamic-filter output path structurally biases toward nonempty responses (a mask token always produces a filter, and similarity maps rarely go uniformly negative), so empty-output supervision fights the architecture rather than the weights, causing outsized interference with normal segmentation.
falsifiable_prediction: Matched PEFT runs with 5-10% empty-prompt supervision will lose significantly more in-domain IoU than runs with equal amounts of hard nonempty supervision, and the degradation will concentrate in low-confidence nonempty cases.
why_important: Prompt-error robustness is mandatory for autonomous cascades; knowing the rejection capability must live outside the mask path (e.g., in a separate head or the IoU head) changes system design.
why_possibly_novel: The observation that SAM cannot abstain is folklore, but a mechanism-level account locating the bias in the dynamic-filter path, plus the interference prediction under PEFT, is unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: PEFT with 0%, 5%, 10% empty-prompt data on one dataset; measure in-domain IoU, empty-detection rate, and whether an alternative (thresholding the IoU head instead) achieves rejection without IoU loss.
main_risk: Degradation could stem from naive loss weighting rather than architecture; requires a tuned-loss control to isolate the structural claim.
default_community_belief: Abstention is a missing training signal: add empty-mask examples and SAM will learn to reject.
why_it_might_be_wrong: With proper loss balance, the decoder may learn uniformly-negative similarity maps easily, and reported instabilities may be reproducible engineering bugs.
fastest_falsification: Three small PEFT runs with varying empty-supervision ratio plus the IoU-head-threshold control: two GPU-days.

one_line: Disagreement between SAM's stability score and its IoU head is an OOD detector: two internal quality signals that decorrelate exactly where the model breaks
problem: There is no accepted label-free way to flag which images in a deployment stream SAM handles badly; single confidence signals fail because they shift with the domain.
core_hypothesis: The stability score (threshold-perturbation robustness of logits) and the learned IoU prediction are computed by different mechanisms with different failure modes; their agreement survives in-distribution but breaks under domain shift, so per-image disagreement is a shift-sensitive alarm.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-image |stability - predicted IoU| will separate in-domain from OOD images with AUROC substantially above either signal alone, and images with high disagreement will have lower true IoU within any fixed domain.
why_important: A zero-training OOD alarm built entirely from signals SAM already computes enables selective human review and targeted data collection for PEFT, with no infrastructure cost.
why_possibly_novel: Both signals exist in the released codebase, but using their disagreement as a calibrated shift detector, benchmarked against standard OOD baselines, appears unpublished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute both signals over one in-domain and three OOD datasets (500 images each), plot per-image disagreement distributions, report AUROC vs each signal alone and vs feature-distance baselines.
main_risk: The two signals may be highly correlated everywhere (both downstream of the same logits), leaving no usable disagreement signal.
default_community_belief: One confidence scalar suffices; OOD detection for segmentation requires external density models or ensembles.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Disagreement may track object difficulty rather than domain shift, flooding the alarm with hard-but-in-domain cases.
fastest_falsification: Signals are already computed by the automatic mask generator; the full analysis is CPU-bound plotting over cached outputs — one day.

one_line: SAM has a measurable minimum segmentable object size (~1.5 patches) that is an architectural constant: adaptation cannot fix it, and knowing the constant redirects effort to input scaling
problem: Teams burn PEFT budget trying to make SAM segment tiny objects, without a principled way to know whether failure is a knowledge gap (fixable by tuning) or an information gap (fixable only by resolution).
core_hypothesis: Below a critical object diameter relative to the 16-pixel patch grid, the encoder provably mixes object and background into the same tokens; the resulting failure is invariant to any weight adaptation and can be characterized as a sharp phase transition in IoU vs object-diameter-in-patches.
falsifiable_prediction: IoU vs object size (in patch units) will show a transition at a constant location across domains and across PEFT strength; fine-tuning will shift performance above the transition but leave the transition point unmoved, while input upsampling will move it.
why_important: A published constant ('SAM cannot segment below X patches, tune all you want') would save the community repeated dead-end adaptation attempts and justify tiling/zooming front-ends as the correct fix.
why_possibly_novel: Small-object failure is well known; the claim that the failure boundary is a domain-invariant architectural constant unaffected by PEFT, established via controlled phase-transition measurement, is the new part.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Synthetic and real objects rescaled to controlled diameters (0.5-6 patches); measure IoU transition for frozen, LoRA-tuned, and heavily-tuned SAM; check invariance of the transition point.
main_risk: The transition may be soft and domain-dependent (contrast interacts with size), undermining the 'constant' framing even if the qualitative story holds.
default_community_belief: With enough domain-specific fine-tuning data, small-object performance keeps improving; failures are data problems.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Sub-patch information does survive in ViT tokens (anti-aliased conv stem, overlapping receptive fields via attention), so tuning might genuinely move the boundary.
fastest_falsification: Synthetic size-sweep on frozen vs one LoRA-tuned checkpoint: two GPU-days to see whether the transition moves.

one_line: Fourier positional encoding of prompts creates sub-pixel grid aliasing: click effectiveness oscillates periodically with position at the patch frequency
problem: Two visually identical clicks a few pixels apart sometimes produce different masks; this is dismissed as noise, but it may be a deterministic aliasing artifact of the prompt positional encoding interacting with the patch grid.
core_hypothesis: The continuous Fourier encoding of click coordinates beats against the discrete 16-pixel token grid, producing a spatially periodic modulation of prompt-image alignment quality with predictable phase and period.
falsifiable_prediction: Averaged over many objects, IoU as a function of click offset modulo 16 pixels will show a statistically significant periodic component (same period and phase across images), rather than being flat as the noise explanation predicts.
why_important: A deterministic ripple can be cancelled for free (snap clicks to favorable phase, or ensemble two half-period-shifted prompts), yielding a universal small gain and a cleaner understanding of prompt-encoder geometry.
why_possibly_novel: Aliasing analyses exist for image classification under translation; a phase-resolved analysis of prompt-coordinate encoding against token-grid alignment in promptable segmentation appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For 300 objects, place clicks on a dense sub-pixel offset grid around a base point, compute mean IoU vs offset-mod-16 heatmap, test for periodicity with a spectral test against shuffled controls.
main_risk: The effect size may be real but tiny (<0.5 IoU points), making it a curiosity rather than a usable lever.
default_community_belief: Click-position sensitivity at the pixel scale is stochastic noise without exploitable structure.
why_it_might_be_wrong: High-frequency Fourier bands may be attenuated enough by learned projections that grid beating never reaches the decoder.
fastest_falsification: Dense offset sweep on 50 objects with spectral analysis: a few GPU-hours; absence of a coherent peak kills it.

one_line: Mask errors cluster at window-attention seams out-of-domain: SAM's windowed ViT blocks leave a spatial fingerprint that adaptation should target, not blur over
problem: SAM's encoder mixes windowed and global attention blocks; if window boundaries create systematic error stripes under domain shift, generic LoRA wastes capacity fixing a spatially structured problem diffusely.
core_hypothesis: Windowed attention creates weaker cross-window feature consistency; in-domain training data taught the global blocks to stitch windows for photographic statistics, and this stitching breaks under domain shift, concentrating errors along the window lattice.
falsifiable_prediction: Averaged OOD error maps (prediction XOR ground truth) will show statistically elevated error density along window-boundary lines compared to phase-shifted control lines, and the elevation will be absent or much weaker in-domain.
why_important: If confirmed, the right adaptation is targeted (tune only global/stitching blocks or add cross-window mixing), which is cheaper and more interpretable than uniform PEFT; it also gives a spatial diagnostic for when this failure is present.
why_possibly_novel: Window-seam artifacts are documented for other hierarchical backbones in generation tasks, but a quantitative seam-aligned error analysis for promptable segmentation under domain shift appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Aggregate error maps over 500 OOD predictions, fold them modulo the window period, run a permutation test for boundary-aligned error elevation vs random foldings; repeat in-domain as control.
main_risk: Object boundaries may correlate with image composition in ways that alias into the window grid, requiring careful null models.
default_community_belief: Global attention blocks fully repair any windowing artifacts; error location is object-driven, not architecture-driven.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The interleaved global blocks may genuinely erase seam effects to below measurable levels even OOD.
fastest_falsification: Folded error-map analysis over cached predictions is pure post-processing: one day, no training.

one_line: Tiling-vs-resizing for high-resolution images interacts with prompt type: point prompts suffer from tiling, box prompts from resizing — an unmeasured 2x2 interaction
problem: Everyone preprocesses large images ad hoc (resize or tile) and reports a single number, but the correct choice may flip depending on the prompt modality the deployment uses.
core_hypothesis: Tiling destroys global context that point prompts need for disambiguation (points are locally ambiguous), while resizing destroys the resolution that makes tight boxes informative (boxes lose their precision advantage), producing a crossover interaction rather than a uniform winner.
falsifiable_prediction: A factorial evaluation (tile/resize x point/box) on high-resolution datasets will show a significant interaction term: tiling beats resizing under box prompts and loses under point prompts, with the crossover magnitude growing with image size.
why_important: It converts an ignored preprocessing choice into a principled, prompt-aware policy that any SAM deployment can apply for free, and it warns benchmark authors that preprocessing choices can reverse method rankings.
why_possibly_novel: Tiling-vs-resizing comparisons exist for detection; conditioning the answer on prompt modality for promptable segmentation, with the interaction as the object of study, appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Two high-resolution datasets, factorial design over preprocessing and prompt type with matched objects, two-way analysis of the IoU results.
main_risk: Effect may be dataset-idiosyncratic (driven by object scale distribution) rather than a general law, requiring at least three diverse sources to claim generality.
default_community_belief: There is one best preprocessing per dataset, independent of how the model will be prompted.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern SAM variants may retain enough context in tiles (large windows) that the point-prompt penalty of tiling is negligible.
fastest_falsification: One dataset, 2x2 factorial with 200 objects: a day of compute, and the absence of interaction is immediately visible.

one_line: Positional-embedding-only tuning after interpolation recovers most of the high-resolution adaptation gain at ~0.01% of parameters
problem: Running SAM above its native resolution requires interpolating positional embeddings, which everyone does naively and then fine-tunes broadly to fix the resulting degradation, without asking whether the damage is confined to the embeddings themselves.
core_hypothesis: Resolution-change degradation is dominated by geometric miscalibration of interpolated positional embeddings (both image-side and prompt-side), not by feature inadequacy, so tuning only PE tables and prompt-coordinate scaling recovers the bulk of the loss.
falsifiable_prediction: At 2x native resolution, PE-only tuning will close >=60% of the gap between naive interpolation and full LoRA on multiple datasets, and its advantage will disappear at native resolution (confirming the mechanism is geometric).
why_important: High-resolution inference is the main lever for small/thin structures; making it nearly free parameter-wise removes a major reason for heavyweight fine-tuning and enables one shared backbone across resolutions.
why_possibly_novel: PE interpolation is standard, but isolating PE re-calibration as a sufficient adaptation for promptable segmentation, including the paired prompt-coordinate encoding, appears unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three datasets at 2x resolution: compare naive interpolation, PE-only tuning, LoRA, and PE+LoRA; report gap closure and confirm the native-resolution null result.
main_risk: Attention patterns themselves (window sizes, relative distances) may break at higher resolution in ways PE tuning cannot express.
default_community_belief: Higher-resolution adaptation requires adapting features throughout the network; PE interpolation is a lossless technicality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For ViTs with window attention the effective receptive-field statistics change with resolution, a global property PE tables cannot repair.
fastest_falsification: One dataset, PE-only vs LoRA at 2x: two GPU-days for a decisive first read.

one_line: Square padding biases masks near the padded side: SAM outputs have a measurable error gradient toward padding, fixable with a learned pad token
problem: SAM pads non-square images to square, and nobody checks whether proximity to the pad region systematically distorts masks, even though padding is a constant unnatural context on one side of many production images.
core_hypothesis: Zero/mean padding produces token statistics unlike any natural context; attention pulls boundary evidence toward or away from the pad region, creating a systematic error gradient as objects approach the padded edge.
falsifiable_prediction: Across wide-format datasets, per-pixel error rate will increase monotonically with proximity to the padded side after controlling for object density, and replacing the pad content with a single learned pad embedding (tuned on a few hundred images) will flatten the gradient.
why_important: Aspect ratios far from square are the norm in documents, panoramas, medical scans, and industrial line cameras; a constant-cost fix that removes a directional bias improves every such deployment.
why_possibly_novel: Padding effects are studied for convolutions; a padding-proximity error analysis and a learned-pad-token fix for promptable ViT segmentation appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take wide images, measure error vs distance-to-pad controlling for distance-to-image-border in the unpadded direction as the control axis; then tune only a pad embedding and re-measure.
main_risk: The gradient may be confounded by content differences near image edges (photographic framing), requiring the controlled comparison to be airtight.
default_community_belief: Padding is a harmless preprocessing detail handled by training-time exposure.
why_it_might_be_wrong: SA-1B contains diverse aspect ratios, so the model may have thoroughly learned to ignore pad regions already.
fastest_falsification: Error-vs-pad-distance regression over cached predictions on one wide-format dataset: hours.

one_line: A pre-adaptation diagnostic that forecasts PEFT gains: the linear-probe gap on frozen SAM features predicts which tasks PEFT can and cannot fix
problem: Teams commit to adaptation projects without any way to predict returns; some tasks jump 20 IoU points with tiny LoRA, others barely move, and the difference is discovered only after spending the budget.
core_hypothesis: SAM's frozen features are boundary-rich but semantics-poor; PEFT succeeds when the target task is limited by decoding (information present, readout wrong) and fails when limited by representation (information absent), and a cheap linear probe on frozen features measures which regime a task is in.
falsifiable_prediction: Across >=8 adaptation tasks, the gap between linear-probe segmentation accuracy and zero-shot SAM accuracy on frozen features will predict realized LoRA gains with high rank correlation, while dataset size and zero-shot IoU alone will predict worse.
why_important: An hour-long forecast replacing week-long trial adaptation changes how adaptation budgets are allocated across an organization's task portfolio.
why_possibly_novel: Linear probing is standard for representation evaluation, but as a predictive instrument for PEFT return-on-investment in promptable segmentation, validated against realized gains, it appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble 8-10 diverse adaptation tasks; for each, compute the probe-vs-zero-shot gap on frozen embeddings, run a standardized LoRA recipe, and correlate predicted vs realized gains.
main_risk: Probe accuracy depends on probe design (resolution, head capacity), risking a self-fulfilling or unstable predictor.
default_community_belief: You cannot know PEFT gains without running PEFT; pilots are the only forecast.
why_it_might_be_wrong: PEFT also changes features (not just readout), so a readout-gap probe may systematically underestimate gains for feature-level fixes.
fastest_falsification: Three tasks with known outcomes, compute the probe gap, check ordering: two GPU-days.

one_line: High-norm artifact tokens in SAM's encoder corrupt decoder cross-attention out-of-domain; learning a handful of register-like sink tokens as the only tuned parameters cleans transfer
problem: Large ViTs are reported to develop high-norm background tokens serving as computation scratchpads; if SAM's encoder has them, the decoder's cross-attention reads them as image content, with unknown consequences that may worsen under domain shift.
core_hypothesis: Artifact tokens are positioned according to in-domain background statistics; under domain shift they relocate unpredictably and attract decoder attention, contributing spatially localized false positives, and appending a few trainable sink tokens (tuned on small OOD data) absorbs this pathological attention.
falsifiable_prediction: Token-norm outliers will exist in SAM's encoder output and their locations will correlate with OOD false-positive blobs; adding 4-8 trained sink tokens will reduce those false positives measurably without changing in-domain behavior.
why_important: It connects a known ViT-internals phenomenon to promptable segmentation quality and yields possibly the smallest useful PEFT ever (a few thousand parameters) targeting a mechanism rather than a dataset.
why_possibly_novel: Register tokens have been proposed for classification backbones at pretraining time; retrofitting them as a post-hoc PEFT for a frozen segmentation foundation model, with a causal link to OOD false positives, appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Map token-norm outliers across in-domain and OOD images, overlay with false-positive locations; then train sink tokens only, on 200 OOD images, and measure false-positive change.
main_risk: SAM's encoder (MAE-initialized, detection-style architecture) may simply lack strong artifact tokens, emptying the premise.
default_community_belief: Encoder token norms are an internal detail; OOD false positives are a data-distribution problem to be fixed with fine-tuning.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Decoder cross-attention may already learn to ignore high-norm tokens via its keys, making sinks redundant.
fastest_falsification: Token-norm mapping plus false-positive overlay requires only forward passes: one day to confirm or refute the correlation premise.

one_line: SAM features are scale-equivariant only inside a 'sweet band' of object sizes; outside it, input rescaling beats any weight-space adaptation
problem: Domains with atypical object scales (aerial, microscopy) get weight-tuned by default, but if the encoder's scale handling is a band-limited property, tuning fights physics that a zoom would fix.
core_hypothesis: The encoder learned approximate scale equivariance only over SA-1B's object-size distribution; log-scale probing will reveal a band where features track rescaling and cliffs outside it, and inside-band domains benefit from PEFT while outside-band domains benefit mainly from input rescaling.
falsifiable_prediction: Feature-similarity curves under controlled input rescaling will show a plateau-plus-cliffs shape with consistent band edges across image content, and adaptation experiments will show weight-tuning gains concentrated inside the band.
why_important: A published scale band gives every practitioner a lookup answer to 'zoom or tune?', one of the most common practical adaptation questions.
why_possibly_novel: Scale generalization is studied for classifiers; a quantitative equivariance-band measurement for a promptable segmenter, tied to a tune-vs-rescale decision rule, appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Rescale a fixed image set over 4 octaves, measure alignment between rescaled features and correspondingly-warped original features per octave; then run matched PEFT on an inside-band and outside-band synthetic task.
main_risk: The band may be soft and content-dependent, making the decision rule too fuzzy to be practical.
default_community_belief: Foundation-model features handle scale; when they do not, fine-tuning fixes it.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Multiscale augmentation during SA-1B training may have produced near-uniform scale handling with no measurable band structure.
fastest_falsification: The feature-similarity-under-rescaling measurement is training-free: one day.

one_line: Domain gap localizes to 2-3 'fracture layers' findable by representation-similarity analysis, and LoRA on only those layers matches full-network LoRA
problem: LoRA placement for SAM is chosen by convention (all attention layers) rather than by measurement, spending parameters uniformly on layers that may not carry the domain gap.
core_hypothesis: Comparing layerwise activation similarity between in-domain and OOD inputs identifies a small set of layers where representations diverge sharply ('fracture layers'); these are where adaptation capacity is needed, and their location is consistent across domains sharing imaging physics.
falsifiable_prediction: Fracture layers identified on unlabeled data will predict the best-performing LoRA placement: fracture-only LoRA will reach >=90% of all-layers LoRA performance at <30% of parameters, and placements on non-fracture layers will underperform at equal budget.
why_important: It replaces placement folklore with a measurement protocol usable before training, and the physics-consistency claim would let placements transfer across related domains without re-analysis.
why_possibly_novel: Representation-similarity tools are established; using them prescriptively for PEFT placement in a promptable segmenter, with validation against realized placement performance, appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For 4 domains, compute layerwise similarity divergence on unlabeled batches, train fracture-only vs all-layers vs random-subset LoRA, compare accuracy-parameter trade-offs.
main_risk: Divergence measured on activations may reflect input statistics (fixable by early layers) rather than where correction is most efficient, decoupling diagnosis from prescription.
default_community_belief: Where you put LoRA matters less than rank and learning rate; all-attention placement is good enough.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Gradient flow can route corrections through almost any layer, so many placements may be near-equivalent, flattening the effect.
fastest_falsification: One domain: divergence profile plus two placement runs (fracture vs anti-fracture): about two GPU-days.

one_line: SAM is strongly shape-biased (trained on masks, not labels), so style/texture augmentation during PEFT is mostly wasted compute — a testable claim against inherited fine-tuning folklore
problem: PEFT recipes for SAM inherit heavy photometric/style augmentation from classification lore, but a mask-supervised model may never have relied on texture in the first place, making these augmentations useless or harmful.
core_hypothesis: Mask-prediction pretraining on SA-1B induced shape-dominant decision rules; SAM's texture reliance is far below ImageNet-classifier levels, so texture-randomizing augmentation neither improves robustness nor transfers, while geometric augmentation retains full value.
falsifiable_prediction: On cue-conflict stimuli (shape of A, texture of B), frozen SAM's masks will follow shape at rates far above classifier baselines; ablating style augmentation from standard PEFT recipes will not degrade OOD segmentation, while ablating geometric augmentation will.
why_important: Augmentation choices multiply training cost and are cargo-culted across the field; measuring what SAM actually relies on trims recipes and clarifies what domain shift means for mask-supervised models.
why_possibly_novel: Shape-vs-texture bias is quantified for classifiers; for promptable mask predictors the bias measurement and its consequence for adaptation augmentation policy appear unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build cue-conflict segmentation stimuli via texture transfer within existing datasets; measure shape-following rate; run PEFT with/without style and with/without geometric augmentation on two OOD tasks.
main_risk: Cue-conflict construction for segmentation is delicate; texture transfer may corrupt boundaries and confound the measurement.
default_community_belief: Strong photometric augmentation is generically good for robustness in any fine-tuning.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Boundary detection is partly a texture-contrast computation, so texture may matter more for masks than for class labels, reversing the prediction.
fastest_falsification: Cue-conflict evaluation on frozen SAM (no training): a couple of days including stimulus construction.

one_line: SAM's decisions ride the phase spectrum: amplitude-spectrum swaps barely change its masks, enabling amplitude-only augmentation as a near-free domain randomizer
problem: Choosing augmentations for PEFT lacks a model-specific principle; if SAM is provably insensitive to amplitude-spectrum statistics, a whole family of cheap frequency-domain augmentations becomes principled rather than heuristic.
core_hypothesis: Object boundary structure lives mainly in the Fourier phase; SAM's mask outputs are approximately invariant to cross-image amplitude swaps, and therefore amplitude randomization during PEFT increases robustness to global-statistics shifts without disturbing the supervision signal.
falsifiable_prediction: Mask IoU between original and amplitude-swapped inputs on frozen SAM will remain high (far above classifier prediction-consistency under the same operation), and PEFT with amplitude randomization will beat standard photometric augmentation on OOD domains characterized by global-statistics shifts.
why_important: It gives a mechanism-grounded, hyperparameter-light augmentation for segmentation adaptation and a clean empirical statement about which image statistics SAM consumes.
why_possibly_novel: Amplitude-swap analysis exists in domain-generalization literature for classifiers; the invariance measurement on a promptable mask model and its use to justify adaptation-time augmentation appears new for this model class.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Amplitude-swap 500 image pairs, measure frozen-SAM mask consistency; then run two PEFT recipes (amplitude-randomized vs photometric) on one global-statistics-shifted domain.
main_risk: Low-level boundary cues have amplitude components (contrast), so invariance may hold for large objects but fail exactly on low-contrast boundaries where it matters.
default_community_belief: Augmentation value is empirical; there is no model-specific frequency-domain principle worth exploiting.
why_it_might_be_wrong: SAM may implicitly use amplitude statistics for figure-ground priors (e.g., sky vs ground), making swaps more disruptive than hypothesized.
fastest_falsification: Frozen-model amplitude-swap consistency on 100 images: hours.

one_line: A single linear 'mask affordance' direction in SAM's feature space predicts whether an object is segmentable at all — triage before you adapt
problem: Failure on a class can mean noisy boundaries (adaptable) or total invisibility to the model (needs different sensing/resolution); there is no cheap per-class instrument distinguishing these before investing in labels.
core_hypothesis: Whether SAM can segment an object is largely determined at the encoder level and is linearly decodable: a direction in pooled-feature space separates objects SAM will segment well from ones it cannot, generalizing across categories and domains.
falsifiable_prediction: A linear classifier trained on frozen pooled features to predict per-object zero-shot IoU>0.5 on one set of domains will transfer to held-out domains with AUROC well above chance and above image-level baselines (contrast, size), indicating a model-internal affordance signal.
why_important: Per-class triage from unlabeled images tells teams which classes PEFT can rescue and which need data-collection changes, before annotation spending.
why_possibly_novel: Predicting a foundation model's own segmentation success from its features, as a transferable one-dimensional affordance, appears unstudied for SAM-class models.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On 4 datasets with GT, compute per-object zero-shot IoU, train the linear predictor on 2 datasets, test transfer on the other 2 against size/contrast baselines.
main_risk: The direction may encode object size and contrast in disguise, adding nothing over trivial baselines.
default_community_belief: Segmentability is a complex interaction of object, context, and prompts; no simple internal signal predicts it.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Success depends heavily on prompt quality and multimask selection, injecting variance no encoder-level signal can capture.
fastest_falsification: The whole pipeline is linear probing over cached features: one to two days.

one_line: Required LoRA rank scales with prompt ambiguity of the task, not dataset size: a scaling study that would rewrite rank-selection practice
problem: Rank is chosen by grid search or copied from papers; without a predictive theory of what drives rank demand, every new task repeats the search and often overspends parameters.
core_hypothesis: Rank demand is driven by the conditional entropy of correct masks given prompts (how many distinct prompt-to-mask behaviors must be learned), not by image diversity or label count; tasks with unambiguous prompts adapt at rank 1-2 regardless of size, ambiguous-prompt tasks need high rank even when small.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a task matrix varying prompt ambiguity and dataset size independently, the rank at which performance saturates will correlate strongly with measured prompt-conditional mask entropy and weakly with dataset size.
why_important: A predictive rank rule eliminates per-task rank searches and reframes LoRA capacity as buying prompt-behavior diversity, a conceptual clarification for all promptable-model PEFT.
why_possibly_novel: LoRA rank studies exist for LLMs with task-difficulty framings; tying rank demand to a measurable prompt-ambiguity statistic in interactive segmentation appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct 3x3 task grid (ambiguity x size) from existing datasets by controlling prompt informativeness (tight box / loose box / center point); sweep ranks {1,2,4,8,16}; locate saturation rank per cell and regress.
main_risk: Prompt ambiguity and boundary complexity may be confounded in real data, requiring synthetic control tasks to separate them.
default_community_belief: Bigger or harder datasets need higher rank; rank is a capacity knob for data volume.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Optimization effects (learning rate interacting with rank) may dominate saturation points, drowning the entropy signal.
fastest_falsification: Two extreme cells (unambiguous-large vs ambiguous-small) with a rank sweep: if unambiguous-large needs the higher rank, the hypothesis dies fast.

one_line: Attention-LoRA moves 'where', FFN-LoRA moves 'what': a functional dissociation in SAM adaptation exploitable as a diagnostic-driven placement rule
problem: Placement choices (QKV vs FFN) are treated as interchangeable knobs; if they fix qualitatively different error types, blind placement wastes budget and mixes remedies.
core_hypothesis: Adapting attention projections primarily changes spatial routing (boundary localization errors), while adapting FFNs primarily changes feature content (missed/hallucinated regions); the error profile of a zero-shot model therefore predicts which placement pays off.
falsifiable_prediction: On tasks whose zero-shot errors are dominated by boundary misplacement, QKV-only LoRA will outperform FFN-only LoRA at equal parameters, and the reverse on tasks dominated by region-level misses; the interaction effect will be significant across >=6 tasks.
why_important: It turns PEFT placement into an evidence-based decision from a cheap error audit, and adds a piece of transferable theory about what different weight families encode in ViT segmenters.
why_possibly_novel: QKV-vs-FFN comparisons exist as ablation tables; connecting them to an error-type taxonomy with predictive power for placement selection appears new for segmentation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Classify zero-shot errors (boundary-F vs region-recall deficits) on 6 tasks, run QKV-only and FFN-only LoRA per task, test the predicted crossover.
main_risk: Both placements may fix both error types through indirect paths, blurring the dissociation below usefulness.
default_community_belief: Placement is a minor hyperparameter; total trainable parameter count is what matters.
why_it_might_be_wrong: In two-way decoders and windowed encoders, spatial routing and content are entangled enough that the clean dissociation from NLP intuitions may not exist.
fastest_falsification: Two tasks with opposite error profiles, two placements each: four runs, about two GPU-days.

one_line: Zero-initialized LoRA B-matrices make the first epochs decoder-dominated, causing decoder overfitting before the encoder ever adapts — fixable with layerwise warmup scheduling
problem: SAM PEFT often plateaus early or overfits with small data, blamed on data scarcity; the real culprit may be an optimization-order artifact built into standard LoRA initialization.
core_hypothesis: Because encoder LoRA contributes zero function change at initialization while decoder gradients are immediately effective, early training commits the decoder to compensations for unadapted features; when encoder adaptation finally arrives, the decoder is in a poor basin, and sequencing (decoder-frozen warmup, then joint) escapes it.
falsifiable_prediction: Tracking per-module gradient norms will show decoder dominance in early steps; a two-phase schedule (encoder-only warmup then joint) will beat standard joint training consistently on small-data adaptation, with the gap shrinking as data grows.
why_important: A free scheduling fix that improves the small-data regime (the regime PEFT exists for) would upgrade every SAM adaptation pipeline without new parameters.
why_possibly_novel: LoRA initialization effects are discussed for LLMs; the encoder-decoder sequencing pathology specific to promptable segmentation architectures, and its scheduling cure, appear unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On 3 small-data tasks (100-500 masks), compare joint vs encoder-first vs decoder-first schedules with matched total steps; log per-module gradient norms to verify the mechanism.
main_risk: Adam's normalization may equalize effective updates quickly enough that the ordering effect is negligible in practice.
default_community_belief: Joint training of all adapters is the default and ordering is irrelevant; small-data failures are data problems.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Decoder-first commitments may be benign or even helpful (fast reduction of easy loss components), not a bad basin.
fastest_falsification: One task, three schedules, gradient-norm logging: one GPU-day.

one_line: LoRA dropout, inherited from NLP recipes, is systematically harmful for prompt-conditioned segmentation
problem: Adapter dropout is copied into SAM fine-tuning configs from language-model defaults without validation; interactive mask decoding may be uniquely brittle to stochastic adapter removal because outputs must remain consistent across prompts on the same image.
core_hypothesis: Dropout on adapter paths injects inconsistency between the prompt-conditioned forward passes that interactive training depends on, acting as label noise on the correction loop rather than as a regularizer, so its optimal value for SAM PEFT is zero.
falsifiable_prediction: Across multiple tasks and data scales, LoRA-dropout sweeps will show monotone degradation with dropout rate for interactive metrics (click curves), even where single-prompt mIoU is flat, contradicting the regularization rationale.
why_important: Recipe hygiene at zero cost: removing a default that actively hurts would improve many published and production configs, and the mechanism (consistency-sensitivity of interactive models) generalizes to other promptable systems.
why_possibly_novel: Nobody appears to have separated single-shot vs interactive metrics when evaluating regularization choices for promptable-model PEFT.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three tasks, dropout in {0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2}, evaluate both single-prompt mIoU and clicks-to-90%-IoU; test for the interactive-metric-specific degradation.
main_risk: At very small data scales dropout may still win by preventing memorization, restricting the claim to a regime rather than a universal.
default_community_belief: Small dropout on adapters is harmless-to-helpful regularization, as in language models.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If interactive training resamples prompts each step anyway, prompt-consistency is already broken by design and dropout adds nothing distinct.
fastest_falsification: One task, four dropout values, click-curve evaluation: one GPU-day.

one_line: Adapter norm growth during training forecasts zero-shot forgetting before any held-out evaluation: an early-stopping signal requiring no generic validation data
problem: Preserving zero-shot breadth while adapting requires held-out generic benchmarks that practitioners rarely maintain; forgetting is discovered after deployment, when generic prompts start failing.
core_hypothesis: The norm trajectory of the learned low-rank update (relative to the frozen weight norms, per layer) tracks how far the function has moved from the pretrained basin; a threshold on normalized update norm predicts measured zero-shot degradation accurately enough to serve as a label-free early-stopping criterion.
falsifiable_prediction: Across many PEFT runs varying task, rank, and learning rate, final zero-shot degradation will correlate strongly with peak normalized adapter norm, and norm-based early stopping will retain most in-domain gain while halving zero-shot loss versus loss-based stopping.
why_important: It converts an invisible cost (breadth loss) into a monitorable training curve, enabling forgetting-aware adaptation without benchmark infrastructure.
why_possibly_novel: Weight-distance-to-pretrained is known to relate to forgetting in full fine-tuning theory; operationalizing adapter-norm telemetry as a practical stopping rule for segmentation PEFT, with validation against realized forgetting, appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run 20 PEFT configurations, record norm trajectories, measure zero-shot IoU on a fixed generic probe set, fit and cross-validate the predictor, then test the stopping rule prospectively on 5 new runs.
main_risk: Norm is direction-blind; small-norm updates in sensitive directions may forget more than large-norm benign ones, capping predictive power.
default_community_belief: Forgetting must be measured behaviorally; training-side signals are too indirect to be actionable.
