why_it_might_be_wrong: Layerwise sensitivity differences may dominate, requiring per-layer calibration that erodes the simplicity that makes the idea attractive.
fastest_falsification: Reanalyze any existing sweep of PEFT runs by correlating final adapter norms with zero-shot scores: no new training if artifacts exist, else ~3 GPU-days.

one_line: Trained LoRAs on SAM collapse to effective rank 1-2 regardless of nominal rank — rank-1 with tuned scale may match rank-16 everywhere
problem: Rank is the headline hyperparameter of LoRA, driving parameter budgets and serving costs, yet nobody checks the spectrum of what training actually learns on segmentation adaptation tasks.
core_hypothesis: The learned update BA has a sharply decaying spectrum (effective rank 1-2) across SAM adaptation tasks; nominal rank mainly rescales optimization dynamics rather than adding used capacity, so rank-1 adapters with adjusted scale and learning rate replicate high-rank results.
falsifiable_prediction: SVD of learned updates across tasks and layers will show >80% spectral energy in the top 1-2 components; truncating trained rank-16 adapters to rank 1 will lose <1 IoU point; rank-1 training with tuned hyperparameters will match rank-16 within noise.
why_important: A 16x reduction in adapter storage and multi-tenant serving memory for free, plus a corrected mental model of what LoRA capacity does in vision adaptation.
why_possibly_novel: Spectrum analyses of learned LoRA updates exist for LLMs with mixed conclusions; the segmentation-adaptation regime (small data, dense outputs) is unmeasured and may behave differently.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect trained adapters from 6 tasks at rank 16, compute spectra, run truncation evaluation, then train rank-1 with a small hyperparameter sweep on 2 tasks for the matching claim.
main_risk: Effective-rank collapse may be an artifact of short training; longer schedules or larger datasets may genuinely populate higher ranks.
default_community_belief: Higher rank means more capacity and better adaptation on harder tasks; rank-16 is a safe default.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense prediction may require higher-dimensional updates than classification-style tasks, making segmentation exactly the place where rank matters.
fastest_falsification: SVD of any existing trained adapters: an hour if artifacts are available; the truncation test is minutes.

one_line: Orthogonality regularization between domain adapters enables interference-free multi-domain serving on one frozen SAM
problem: Serving many domain adapters on shared infrastructure invites cross-talk when adapters are merged or hot-swapped approximately; independently trained adapters occupy overlapping subspaces and cannot be composed safely.
core_hypothesis: Training each domain's low-rank update inside a subspace orthogonal to previously allocated ones costs little per-domain accuracy (the adaptation manifold is low-dimensional relative to weight space) and buys near-zero interference under merging, enabling a single merged multi-domain model.
falsifiable_prediction: Jointly-orthogonalized adapters will lose <1 IoU point per domain versus unconstrained training, while their merged sum will retain per-domain performance dramatically better than merged unconstrained adapters, with the advantage growing in the number of domains.
why_important: One merged model serving N domains removes routing infrastructure and latency; the geometric picture (how much orthogonal capacity SAM's weight space offers) is a foundational measurement for adapter ecosystems.
why_possibly_novel: Orthogonal adapter ideas exist in continual learning for classifiers; measuring the capacity-interference trade-off for segmentation foundation models under explicit merging, as a serving strategy, appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train 4 domain adapters unconstrained vs orthogonalized; evaluate individually and merged; sweep number of domains from 2 to 4 to observe interference scaling.
main_risk: Related domains may need overlapping directions (shared physics), making orthogonality actively harmful exactly for adapter families likely to be co-served.
default_community_belief: Multi-domain serving requires either routing to separate adapters or accepting merge degradation; interference is unavoidable.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Low-rank orthogonality in parameter space does not guarantee functional non-interference, since different weight directions can affect the same functional behaviors.
fastest_falsification: Two domains, both regimes, merge and evaluate: about two GPU-days.

one_line: Contradictory 'LoRA works/doesn't work on SAM' findings trace to the alpha/rank scale factor: a meta-scientific audit with a corrective recipe
problem: The literature and practitioner reports disagree wildly on whether encoder LoRA helps SAM; if a single mis-set scale hyperparameter explains the disagreement, the field is aggregating noise into folklore.
core_hypothesis: The effective update magnitude (alpha/rank times learned norm) is the dominant determinant of reported outcomes; re-running published-style configurations with a proper scale sweep will reverse a substantial fraction of negative conclusions and homogenize positive ones.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a matrix of replicated configurations from public recipes, outcome variance attributable to scale will exceed variance attributable to placement, rank, and dataset choice combined, and previously 'failed' settings will succeed after scale correction in a majority of cases.
why_important: Correcting a field-wide confounder prevents wasted research directions premised on 'LoRA fails for segmentation encoders' and establishes reporting standards (always state effective scale).
why_possibly_novel: Hyperparameter-sensitivity meta-analyses exist for deep RL and LLM evaluation; nobody has run the equivalent audit for vision-foundation-model PEFT claims.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect 6 public SAM-LoRA configurations with divergent conclusions, re-run each with a 5-point scale sweep on 2 shared datasets, decompose outcome variance by factor.
main_risk: Reproduction fidelity: differences in data processing and prompt simulation across recipes may prevent clean attribution to scale.
default_community_belief: Divergent LoRA-on-SAM results reflect genuine task differences; hyperparameters were adequately tuned in published work.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The disagreements may instead trace to prompt-simulation differences or evaluation protocol (oracle vs realistic prompts), not scale.
fastest_falsification: Take one 'LoRA fails' configuration and sweep scale: if failure persists across the sweep, the single-confounder story is dead — one GPU-day.

one_line: Bias-only tuning of SAM's neck convolutions is the highest-leverage parameters-per-point site in the whole model
problem: The neck (the small convolutional projection from ViT tokens to the 256-channel embedding the decoder consumes) is the narrowest waist in SAM, yet placement studies ignore it in favor of encoder blocks with orders of magnitude more parameters.
core_hypothesis: Because every bit of decoder-visible information passes through the neck, small affine corrections there (biases and per-channel scales, a few thousand parameters) can re-weight feature channels for a new domain more efficiently than any encoder-internal adaptation of equal size.
falsifiable_prediction: Neck bias+scale tuning will dominate the parameter-efficiency frontier: at <10k trainable parameters it will beat rank-1 encoder LoRA and match rank-4 on the majority of moderate domain shifts, failing only on shifts requiring new feature computation.
why_important: An extreme-low-budget adaptation site that reuses cached ViT activations (the neck is after the expensive part) makes per-session personalization computationally trivial.
why_possibly_novel: BitFit-style bias tuning is known for transformers generally; identifying the neck as the singular high-leverage waist in promptable segmenters, with the caching corollary, appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On 5 domain shifts of varying severity, compare neck-affine tuning vs encoder LoRA ranks {1,4} at matched and unmatched parameter counts; map where the neck option wins.
main_risk: Channel re-weighting may be too coarse for spatially structured shifts, restricting wins to global-statistics domains only.
default_community_belief: Meaningful adaptation capacity lives in the big encoder; tiny post-hoc affine layers are toys.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If domain shifts mostly require new local feature detectors, no amount of channel re-weighting at the waist can synthesize them.
fastest_falsification: One moderate shift, neck-affine vs rank-1 LoRA: under one GPU-day using cached embeddings for the neck variant.

one_line: LayerNorm-affine-only tuning acts as 'domain whitening' and wins specifically where the shift is global (contrast inversion, intensity remapping) with tiny labeled sets
problem: For globally-shifted modalities practitioners deploy full LoRA and overfit their few labels; the minimal sufficient adaptation for statistics-level shifts has not been isolated for promptable segmenters.
core_hypothesis: Global photometric shifts move activation statistics in ways correctable by per-layer affine parameters alone; LN-affine tuning implements input-conditional whitening with ~0.05% of parameters and an inductive bias that cannot overfit spatial idiosyncrasies of small datasets.
falsifiable_prediction: On synthetic global shifts (inversion, gamma, histogram remap) LN-only tuning will match full LoRA within 1 IoU point using 50 labels, while on spatially structured shifts it will clearly lose; the win/loss boundary will be predictable from a two-sample test on channelwise activation statistics.
why_important: It creates a decision rule (measure the shift type, choose the minimal adapter) replacing one-size-fits-all PEFT, particularly valuable in label-starved scientific imaging.
why_possibly_novel: LN-tuning is a known cheap baseline; the contribution is the shift-type-conditional theory of when it suffices, with a measurable predictor, for segmentation foundation models.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct 4 synthetic global shifts and 2 spatial shifts on the same base dataset; compare LN-only vs LoRA at 50/200/1000 labels; validate the statistics-based predictor of which regime holds.
main_risk: Real-world shifts are rarely purely global, so the clean regime boundary may dissolve in practice.
default_community_belief: More trainable parameters never hurt if regularized; LoRA is the safe default for any shift.
why_it_might_be_wrong: At 50 labels even LoRA rarely overfits with early stopping, potentially erasing LN's small-data advantage.
fastest_falsification: One inversion-shift dataset at 50 labels, LN-only vs LoRA: single GPU-day.

one_line: Box-prompt and point-prompt supervision pull SAM's encoder in measurably conflicting directions during PEFT — prompt-type-conditioned adapters remove the conflict
problem: Adaptation datasets mix prompt types for robustness, assuming the objectives cooperate; if they conflict at the gradient level, mixed training silently caps both capabilities.
core_hypothesis: Box-conditioned and point-conditioned tasks demand different feature trade-offs (boundary precision inside a known extent vs global disambiguation of an unknown extent); during PEFT their gradient directions on shared adapters have negative cosine similarity on a meaningful fraction of steps, and routing them to separate small adapters lifts both.
falsifiable_prediction: Measured per-step cosine similarity between prompt-type gradient components will be negative significantly more often than a label-split control; two prompt-conditioned adapters (same total parameters as one shared) will beat shared training on both prompt-type test sets.
why_important: Prompt-conditioned routing is nearly free at inference (prompt type is known) and would become a standard trick; the conflict measurement itself explains a chunk of unexplained PEFT underperformance.
why_possibly_novel: Gradient-conflict analysis is established for multi-task learning; treating prompt modality as the task variable in promptable-model adaptation appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument gradient cosines during mixed-prompt PEFT on 2 datasets; then train shared vs prompt-routed adapters at matched parameters and compare per-prompt-type metrics.
main_risk: Conflict may concentrate in a few layers only, making full routing overkill and the effect size small.
default_community_belief: Mixing prompt types is pure positive augmentation, teaching robustness with no cost.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Both objectives share the same ground-truth masks, so their gradients may align almost everywhere except trivial components.
fastest_falsification: Gradient-cosine logging inside an existing training loop: hours of engineering, one training run.

one_line: Mask loss and IoU-head loss conflict at the gradient level during PEFT; detaching the quality head into a second phase fixes calibration collapse for free
problem: Standard SAM fine-tuning jointly optimizes mask quality and the quality-prediction head through shared decoder features; if these objectives interfere, both mask accuracy ceilings and calibration are silently degraded.
core_hypothesis: The IoU-regression gradient reshapes shared decoder features toward variance-reduction (good for prediction, bad for sharp boundaries), producing measurable negative gradient cosine with the mask loss; a two-phase schedule (masks first, then calibrate the detached head) achieves better values of both objectives than joint training.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-step gradient cosine between the two losses on shared parameters will be negative substantially more often than a random-split control, and two-phase training will simultaneously improve final mIoU and expected calibration error versus tuned joint baselines.
why_important: Every SAM fine-tune inherits this joint loss from the original recipe without question; a scheduling fix improving both metrics would propagate to all downstream adaptation work.
why_possibly_novel: Multi-task interference is well studied, but nobody appears to have audited the specific mask/IoU-head coupling inside SAM-style decoders during adaptation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument both gradients during standard PEFT on two datasets; then compare joint vs two-phase vs weighted variants at matched compute, reporting mIoU and ECE.
main_risk: Interference may be too weak to matter at typical loss weights, making the fix a no-op in practice.
default_community_belief: The original SAM joint loss is a settled, benign design; fine-tuning recipes should replicate it.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The IoU head is small and its gradient contribution to shared features may be negligible compared to the mask loss.
fastest_falsification: Gradient-cosine logging in one training run: hours to see whether conflict exists at all.

one_line: The popular batch-norm test-time-adaptation family silently no-ops on SAM (LayerNorm has no batch statistics) — an audit of TTA methods that vision practitioners port without checking
problem: TTA literature is dominated by tricks that recompute or adapt normalization statistics; practitioners port these to SAM-based pipelines, but LayerNorm computes statistics per-token at inference already, so several celebrated methods reduce to identity or to something unintended.
core_hypothesis: A systematic audit will find that a substantial fraction of published TTA gains claimed or assumed for segmentation foundation models cannot apply mechanistically to LN-based promptable models, and reported improvements in such pipelines trace to other components (augmentation, thresholds) rather than the normalization adaptation.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-implementations of BN-statistic TTA on SAM will show exactly zero functional change where methods only touch batch statistics, and ablations of hybrid pipelines will attribute their gains to non-normalization components.
why_important: It prevents a wave of confused engineering and redirects TTA research for promptable segmenters toward levers that exist (LN affine parameters, prompt-space adaptation, logit priors).
why_possibly_novel: The mechanical incompatibility is obvious once stated but appears unstated: pipelines and blog-level practice keep including BN-adaptation steps for ViT/SAM systems.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Survey 10 TTA methods, classify their mechanism, run the mechanistically-inapplicable ones on SAM verifying zero deltas, then ablate one hybrid pipeline end-to-end.
main_risk: The strawman risk: sophisticated practitioners may already avoid this, making the audit's target population smaller than assumed.
default_community_belief: Normalization-based TTA is a generic tool applicable to any deep segmentation model.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If most real pipelines already use LN-affine variants correctly, the audit finds no live confusion and reduces to a footnote.
fastest_falsification: Check three popular TTA repos for SAM compatibility claims and run one: a day.

one_line: A per-block leave-one-in LoRA atlas for SAM: most adaptation gain concentrates in 2 specific blocks, publishable as a reusable placement map
problem: Placement studies report coarse contrasts (encoder vs decoder, QKV vs FFN) but no block-resolution map exists showing where in SAM's depth adaptation capacity actually pays, so every practitioner re-guesses.
core_hypothesis: Leave-one-in experiments (LoRA on a single block at a time) will reveal a sparse structure: a small set of blocks (hypothesized: the earliest blocks handling low-level statistics and the final global-attention block feeding the neck) captures the large majority of achievable gain, consistently across domains with similar shift types.
falsifiable_prediction: The block-gain profile will be far from uniform (top-2 blocks capturing >60% of the all-blocks gain), and profiles will cluster by shift type across datasets, enabling placement transfer to unseen domains of a known type.
why_important: A published atlas converts placement from per-project search into table lookup, saving the community large amounts of repeated compute, and the profile shape itself is evidence about where domain information lives.
why_possibly_novel: Block-granular leave-one-in mapping with cross-domain clustering, for promptable segmentation, appears not to exist publicly.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On 3 datasets, run single-block LoRA for every encoder block plus decoder, at fixed rank and schedule; plot gain profiles; test top-2-block placement against all-blocks on a 4th dataset.
main_risk: Single-block gains may not compose (interactions between blocks), weakening the atlas as a prescription even if the map is accurate descriptively.
default_community_belief: Spreading LoRA across all attention layers is near-optimal; block-level structure is second-order.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Residual networks distribute functionality; gains may genuinely be flat across blocks, making the atlas trivial and uniform.
fastest_falsification: One dataset, ~30 single-block runs at small scale: parallelizable to under a day on a small cluster; a flat profile ends the project early.

one_line: Weight decay on LoRA parameters is a continuous forgetting knob: because decay pulls toward the zero-update (pretrained) function, one scalar trades in-domain gain against zero-shot retention smoothly
problem: Practitioners need a controllable dial between specialization and breadth but currently manage forgetting with ad hoc tricks (early stopping, data mixing) that are hard to tune and reason about.
core_hypothesis: Since LoRA parameterizes the deviation from pretrained weights, standard L2 decay on adapter parameters is exactly a regularizer toward the zero-shot function; sweeping it traces a smooth, monotone Pareto front between in-domain IoU and zero-shot retention, more stable than early stopping.
falsifiable_prediction: Across tasks, varying only adapter weight decay will produce a smooth Pareto curve whose extremes bracket early-stopping-based operating points, with lower variance across seeds than epoch-based selection at matched retention levels.
why_important: A one-parameter, optimizer-native forgetting control that requires no replay data or extra evaluation infrastructure would become the default breadth-preservation mechanism for adapter fine-tuning.
why_possibly_novel: The observation that decay-on-delta equals pull-toward-pretrained is mathematically elementary, but its systematic use and validation as a forgetting dial for segmentation PEFT appears unexploited.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three tasks, weight-decay sweep over 5 values with fixed schedule, measure in-domain IoU and generic zero-shot probe IoU per value, across 3 seeds; compare front smoothness vs early-stopping selection.
main_risk: Decay interacts with Adam in nonstandard ways (decoupled vs coupled), possibly making the dial non-monotone at practical settings.
default_community_belief: Forgetting management requires replay data, regularization toward feature-space anchors, or careful early stopping.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The zero-update point preserves the function, but small decays may sit in flat regions doing nothing until a cliff, breaking smoothness.
fastest_falsification: One task, five decay values, both metrics: one to two GPU-days.

one_line: Merging sequential-task adapters by concatenate-then-SVD-truncate retains both tasks better than weight averaging: a testable claim about the geometry of segmentation adapters
problem: Users accumulate adapters over time (task A, then task B) and want one deployable artifact; naive averaging degrades both tasks unpredictably, and there is no validated merging recipe for segmentation adapters.
core_hypothesis: Adapter updates for distinct segmentation tasks occupy partially disjoint low-rank subspaces; stacking the low-rank factors and truncating via SVD preserves each task's principal directions where averaging destructively interferes mid-subspace, so SVD merging dominates averaging at equal final rank.
falsifiable_prediction: Across task pairs, SVD-merged adapters at rank r will beat averaged adapters at the same effective rank on the minimum of the two task scores, with the margin growing as inter-task subspace principal angles grow.
why_important: A reliable merge operation is the missing primitive for adapter version control, federated contribution, and continual deployment without model zoos.
why_possibly_novel: Model-merging research focuses on full weights or classifier heads; rank-aware merging of segmentation adapters with a subspace-angle-based predictor of merge quality appears open.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Six task pairs of varying relatedness; merge by average and by concat-SVD at matched ranks; regress the merge-quality gap on measured principal angles.
main_risk: Both merging schemes may fail badly for genuinely conflicting tasks, making the comparison moot where it matters most.
default_community_belief: Averaging is the default merge; anything fancier is marginal.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Nonlinear interactions through the frozen network can make parameter-space subspace preservation irrelevant to functional retention.
fastest_falsification: One related and one unrelated task pair, both merges: a day, given trained adapters.

one_line: 4-bit quantization of SAM's encoder damages boundary F-score disproportionately versus region IoU: quantization noise is high-frequency and boundaries live there
problem: QLoRA-style pipelines (quantized backbone plus adapters) are being ported to SAM for cheap adaptation, validated only on region-level IoU, which may hide a systematic boundary-quality tax.
core_hypothesis: Weight quantization noise perturbs high-spatial-frequency feature content more than low-frequency content; since region IoU is dominated by object interiors and boundary-F by high-frequency structure, quantization will produce a signature metric divergence that region-level evaluations cannot see.
falsifiable_prediction: Across bit-widths {16, 8, 4}, region mIoU will degrade mildly and roughly linearly while boundary-F degrades super-linearly below 8 bits, and the divergence will be strongest for thin and small structures; adapter training on top will recover region metrics faster than boundary metrics.
why_important: Quantized adaptation is the default cost-saving path to deployment; if it selectively sacrifices boundaries, boundary-critical applications need different compression (or boundary-aware calibration), and evaluation standards must include boundary metrics.
why_possibly_novel: Quantization studies report task-level accuracy; a frequency-decomposed analysis of what quantization costs promptable segmentation appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Quantize the encoder at 3 bit-widths, evaluate region and boundary metrics on 3 datasets stratified by structure thickness, then run identical LoRA adaptation on each and compare recovery rates per metric.
main_risk: Modern quantizers with outlier handling may be gentle enough that the effect exists only below 4 bits where nobody operates.
default_community_belief: 4-bit backbones with adapters match full precision for practical purposes; region mIoU parity means parity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Boundary quality may be dominated by the (unquantized) decoder and upscaler, insulating it from encoder quantization noise.
fastest_falsification: One dataset, three bit-widths, both metric families: one day with existing quantization tooling.

one_line: Anchor-prompt rehearsal: storing ~100 (image-embedding, prompt, mask) triplets and replaying them in embedding space prevents forgetting at near-zero cost — no images retained
problem: Replay is the most reliable anti-forgetting tool but retaining raw pretraining-like images is heavy and often legally impossible; SAM's architecture (frozen-computable embeddings, tiny decoder) may permit replay without images.
core_hypothesis: Forgetting in SAM PEFT is concentrated in decoder-visible function space; replaying a very small set of cached embedding-prompt-mask anchors through the decoder path during adaptation regularizes exactly the function that degrades, and 100 anchors suffice because the decoder is small.
falsifiable_prediction: PEFT with 100-anchor embedding replay will retain >90% of zero-shot generic performance while matching no-replay adaptation in-domain, outperforming weight-decay and early-stopping baselines at matched in-domain accuracy; benefits will saturate rapidly with anchor count.
why_important: A kilobyte-scale, privacy-compatible rehearsal recipe would make breadth-preserving adaptation the default rather than a luxury, especially in regulated domains.
why_possibly_novel: Replay in feature space exists in continual learning; exploiting a promptable architecture's cached-embedding structure for anchor-based rehearsal of an interactive function appears specific and new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select anchors by stratified sampling from a generic dataset; run PEFT with/without replay on 3 tasks; report retention and in-domain metrics vs baselines; sweep anchor count {10, 100, 1000}.
main_risk: If forgetting happens in encoder adapters (feature drift), decoder-path replay with frozen cached embeddings cannot see or prevent it.
default_community_belief: Meaningful rehearsal requires substantial stored data approximating the pretraining distribution.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Embeddings cached from the frozen encoder become stale the moment encoder adapters train, invalidating the replay signal precisely when it is needed.
fastest_falsification: One task with encoder-frozen decoder-tuned PEFT plus replay: if retention does not improve even in this most favorable case, the idea dies — one GPU-day.

one_line: Forgetting in adapted SAM is prompt-channel-selective: box-task PEFT degrades point-prompt zero-shot far more than box zero-shot
problem: Zero-shot degradation after adaptation is reported as one number, hiding which capabilities were lost; if forgetting has prompt-type structure, single-number reports systematically mislead deployment decisions.
core_hypothesis: Adaptation reshapes the decoder's use of prompt tokens toward the trained prompt distribution; capabilities tied to undertrained prompt channels decay first, so a model tuned exclusively with boxes remains a good zero-shot box model while silently becoming a poor click model (and vice versa).
falsifiable_prediction: In a factorial study (train prompt type x eval prompt type, on held-out generic data), the interaction term will be large: same-type zero-shot retention will exceed cross-type retention by a wide margin, consistently across tasks and PEFT methods.
why_important: Teams tune with whatever prompts are convenient and deploy interactive tools assuming generic interactivity survived; channel-selective forgetting would mandate matching training prompts to deployment prompts or mixing deliberately.
why_possibly_novel: Forgetting studies for segmentation track datasets and classes; prompt modality as the axis of forgetting appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Adapt SAM on 2 tasks under box-only, point-only, and mixed prompting; evaluate zero-shot on generic data with both prompt types; quantify the interaction.
main_risk: Decoder capacity may be large enough that both channels survive typical small-data PEFT, making the effect real but negligible at practical scales.
default_community_belief: Zero-shot degradation is a scalar property of how hard you fine-tuned, not structured by prompt modality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Prompt tokens share most decoder pathways, so degradation may be strongly correlated across channels after all.
fastest_falsification: One task, box-only training, evaluate both prompt types zero-shot: one GPU-day for a first read on the interaction.

one_line: Adapter scale interpolation at inference (alpha from 0 to 1) traces a smooth in-domain/zero-shot Pareto family from a single trained adapter — one training run, a continuum of models
problem: Different consumers of the same adapted model need different specialization levels (a hospital wants max in-domain, a research tool wants breadth), currently requiring separate training runs per operating point.
core_hypothesis: The linear path from zero adapter to full adapter in weight space corresponds to a monotone, low-loss path in function space (no barrier), because LoRA updates are small and the pretrained basin is locally convex-ish; therefore post-hoc alpha scaling yields valid intermediate models without any retraining.
falsifiable_prediction: Sweeping the adapter scale on trained adapters will produce monotone in-domain and zero-shot curves (no non-monotonic dips) for the large majority of tasks, and the alpha-family will Pareto-dominate early-stopping checkpoints of the same run.
why_important: Deployment-time specialization control (even per-request) from a single artifact simplifies MLOps for adapter ecosystems substantially.
why_possibly_novel: Weight interpolation between checkpoints is studied for full models; validating the scale-interpolation family as a deployment mechanism for segmentation adapters, against retrained baselines, appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For 5 tasks, sweep alpha in [0,1.25] on trained adapters, measure both metrics, compare the traced front against 5 early-stopping checkpoints and 3 retrained lower-LR baselines.
main_risk: Nonlinear interactions (LayerNorm downstream of scaled updates) may create non-monotone behavior for some layers, breaking the clean family on some tasks.
default_community_belief: Operating points along the specialization-breadth trade-off require separate training or explicit multi-objective methods.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The function path may pass through regions worse than both endpoints (interpolation barrier), as observed for some full fine-tuning settings.
fastest_falsification: Alpha sweep on any existing trained adapter: an hour of inference.

one_line: Fine-tuned SAM loses 'ambiguity honesty': its three mask hypotheses collapse into near-duplicates, and nobody measures this collapse
problem: SAM's multimask output exists to represent genuine ambiguity (part vs whole); adaptation on single-granularity labels may quietly destroy this capability, harming downstream interactive use even when headline mIoU improves.
core_hypothesis: Single-target supervision teaches all mask tokens to chase the same answer; diversity of the multimask set (pairwise IoU distances) collapses early in fine-tuning, and this collapse is a distinct, measurable forgetting mode that replaying ambiguous prompts prevents cheaply.
falsifiable_prediction: Multimask diversity on ambiguous generic prompts (e.g., clicks on part-whole structures) will drop by a large factor after standard PEFT while mIoU on the target task rises; a small replay of ambiguous cases will preserve diversity at negligible in-domain cost.
why_important: Interactive tools rely on offering alternatives when prompts are ambiguous; shipping adapted models that silently lost this behavior degrades user experience in ways current metrics cannot detect, so the metric itself is a contribution.
why_possibly_novel: Output-diversity collapse under fine-tuning is discussed for generative models; defining and tracking it for promptable segmentation's hypothesis set appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define a diversity metric over the 3-mask set on a fixed ambiguous-prompt probe suite; measure before/after adaptation across 4 recipes; test the ambiguous-replay mitigation.
main_risk: Diversity may be worthless for the adapted deployment (single-granularity tasks), making the loss real but irrelevant for those users.
default_community_belief: Multimask behavior is an inference detail; adaptation quality equals target-task mIoU.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The multimask heads may be robust because their token embeddings are barely updated by typical decoder-light PEFT recipes.
fastest_falsification: Diversity probe before/after any single existing fine-tune: hours with cached models.

one_line: Domain-adapted SAM gets worse at being corrected: first-click accuracy rises but the refinement loop breaks, visible only in click-curve evaluation
problem: Adaptation is validated on single-shot metrics, but deployed SAM is interactive; if fine-tuning trades correction-responsiveness for first-shot accuracy, evaluations systematically prefer models that are worse in real use.
core_hypothesis: Interactive robustness (proper response to corrective clicks and logit feedback) is a distinct learned skill acquired from SA-1B's interactive training stage; single-shot supervised PEFT overwrites it, so adapted models show flatter or even inverted click curves despite higher first-click IoU.
falsifiable_prediction: On adapted models, clicks-to-95%-IoU will worsen relative to zero-shot SAM on a meaningful fraction of tasks even where 1-click IoU improved, and adding simulated interactive training to PEFT will restore curve slope at small cost to first-click gains.
why_important: If confirmed, the field's default evaluation is optimizing the wrong objective for interactive deployments, and interactive simulation must enter every adaptation recipe — a practice-changing result.
why_possibly_novel: Click curves exist in interactive-segmentation literature, but auditing adaptation methods for refinement-loop damage appears not to be standard or published for foundation segmenters.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For 4 adaptation recipes on 3 datasets, evaluate full click curves (1-10 clicks) for zero-shot vs adapted models under an identical simulator; compare curve slopes and crossings.
main_risk: Click simulators may diverge from human behavior enough that curve damage measured in simulation misestimates real-use damage in either direction.
default_community_belief: Higher single-shot accuracy implies a better interactive model; refinement ability is preserved by default.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Refinement may be implemented by prompt-encoder and dense-prompt pathways that typical PEFT leaves frozen, insulating the loop from damage.
fastest_falsification: Click-curve evaluation of one existing adapted checkpoint vs its base: a few hours.

one_line: SAM's stability score beats its IoU head as a pseudo-label filter for self-training: the untrained signal outperforms the trained one out-of-domain
problem: Self-training on SAM pseudo-masks is the standard label-free adaptation route, and everyone filters candidates by IoU-head confidence, which is precisely the component most miscalibrated under domain shift.
core_hypothesis: The stability score (a structural property: robustness of the mask to logit-threshold perturbation) degrades more gracefully OOD than the learned IoU regression, so stability-filtered pseudo-label sets have higher precision at matched volume and yield better student adapters.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched pseudo-label acceptance rates on OOD data, stability-filtered sets will show higher true-quality precision, and PEFT on them will outperform confidence-filtered self-training consistently across domains.
why_important: A one-line change (swap the filtering scalar) improving the most common unsupervised adaptation pipeline is immediately actionable for every practitioner.
why_possibly_novel: Both scores ship with SAM's mask generator; a controlled comparison as pseudo-label filters for domain adaptation, with the OOD-robustness framing, appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On 3 OOD datasets with hidden GT: generate pseudo-masks, filter by each score at matched volumes, measure precision, then train adapters per condition and compare downstream IoU.
main_risk: The two scores are correlated; matched-volume differences may be too small to change downstream results meaningfully.
default_community_belief: The learned quality head is the principled filter; stability is an auxiliary heuristic for mask deduplication.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Stability can be high for confidently-wrong masks (clean but incorrect boundaries), a failure mode the IoU head sometimes catches.
fastest_falsification: Precision-at-matched-volume comparison on one OOD dataset with labels: a day, no training needed for the first verdict.

one_line: Single-image TTA for SAM: enforce mask consistency across jittered prompts, updating only LayerNorm affines — adaptation from one unlabeled test image
problem: Many deployments see novel domains one image at a time (field robotics, rare scanners) where batch adaptation is impossible; SAM has no accepted single-image adaptation mechanism.
core_hypothesis: Disagreement among masks produced by slightly-perturbed equivalent prompts is a self-supervised error signal specific to promptable models; minimizing it over a handful of LN-affine parameters per test image reduces genuine errors rather than collapsing to trivial solutions, because the frozen prompt-decoder pathway anchors the objective.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-image jitter-consistency optimization (5-20 gradient steps) will improve true IoU on the majority of OOD images with degraded zero-shot performance, will rarely hurt in-domain images, and collapse (empty/full masks) will not occur while updates are restricted to LN affines.
why_important: Prompt-equivariance is a supervision source that only promptable models possess; validating it would open a TTA family unavailable to classic segmenters and useful at the single-image extreme.
why_possibly_novel: Consistency-based TTA exists for augmentations of the input image; using the prompt channel as the perturbation axis, with parameter-restricted updates, appears specific to this model class and unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On 200 OOD images, run per-image optimization with jittered clicks and boxes; report IoU deltas versus zero-shot, plus collapse statistics and in-domain no-harm checks.
main_risk: The model can satisfy consistency by becoming prompt-insensitive in the wrong way (same wrong mask for all prompts), and LN-restriction may not fully prevent this.
default_community_belief: TTA needs batches of target data; single-image adaptation of a large segmenter is too unstable to be useful.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Jitter-consistency may already be high OOD (stable but wrong), providing no gradient toward correctness.
fastest_falsification: Correlation check first: does jitter-inconsistency correlate with true error per image? Pure inference, hours; no correlation kills the objective.

one_line: Cyclic prompt-mask self-supervision: derive prompts from SAM's own output mask, re-predict, and demand a fixed point — a label-free adaptation loss with a built-in sanity semantics
problem: Unsupervised adaptation losses for segmentation (entropy, pseudo-labels) import assumptions from classification and often collapse; promptable models offer an unexploited structural invariance: a correct mask should be recoverable from prompts derived from itself.
core_hypothesis: For well-segmented objects, prompts synthesized from the predicted mask (centroid click, tight box) regenerate nearly the same mask (cycle-consistency), while errors amplify through the cycle; minimizing cycle divergence on unlabeled target data adapts the model toward self-coherent segmentations that correlate with true quality.
falsifiable_prediction: Cycle divergence will correlate with true IoU across OOD images (validation of the signal), and adapters trained to minimize it on unlabeled data will improve true IoU on held-out target images versus entropy-minimization and pseudo-label baselines at matched compute.
why_important: A native self-supervision principle for promptable segmenters would make label-free adaptation more principled and portable across SAM-family models, replacing borrowed classification losses.
why_possibly_novel: Cycle-consistency is classic in registration and translation; instantiating it through the prompt interface of a segmentation foundation model as a training objective appears novel.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Step 1: measure cycle-divergence vs true-IoU correlation on 3 OOD datasets (inference only). Step 2: train LN/LoRA-light adapters on the cycle loss for the best-correlating domain, compare against baselines.
main_risk: Degenerate fixed points exist (e.g., blob-shaped masks reproduce themselves easily), and the loss may reward simplification rather than correctness.
default_community_belief: Unsupervised segmentation adaptation means entropy minimization or self-training; there is no additional structure to exploit.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Cycle stability may be necessary but far from sufficient for correctness, giving a well-correlated signal that nonetheless optimizes toward blandness.
fastest_falsification: The correlation study is pure inference over cached predictions: one day decides whether the loss candidate has signal.

one_line: Multimask-entropy as a TTA stopping criterion: stop adapting when hypothesis diversity stops shrinking — a label-free convergence detector
problem: Test-time adaptation famously lacks a stopping rule; without labels, methods over-adapt and collapse, and current practice picks step counts by superstition.
core_hypothesis: During beneficial adaptation, SAM's multimask hypothesis set contracts (ambiguity resolves) and then plateaus; continued optimization past the plateau signals objective-hacking rather than learning, so the knee of the diversity curve is a domain-agnostic stopping point.
falsifiable_prediction: Across TTA methods and domains, true-IoU trajectories will peak within a small window around the multimask-diversity plateau knee, and knee-based stopping will retain most of the oracle-stopping gain while fixed-step baselines lose substantially more.
why_important: A reliable label-free stopping rule removes the biggest deployment blocker for TTA on segmentation models, and the diagnostic uses outputs SAM already produces.
why_possibly_novel: Stopping criteria via internal-signal plateaus have been tried with entropy in classification; using the promptable model's hypothesis-set geometry as the convergence witness appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run 3 TTA objectives on 3 domains, log true IoU (hidden) and diversity per step, measure peak-to-knee offsets, then prospectively apply knee-stopping on 2 new domains.
main_risk: Diversity may plateau immediately (prompt-insensitive collapse) or oscillate, producing false knees that stop adaptation too early.
default_community_belief: TTA stopping is unsolved; fixed small step counts are the least-bad option.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The diversity signal may track the adaptation objective rather than true quality, making the knee coincide with collapse instead of preceding it.
fastest_falsification: Log diversity during any existing TTA run with hidden labels: near-zero extra cost; misaligned knees on the first domain kill it.

one_line: Training-free adaptation by memory: retrieve nearest SA-1B-like embedding neighborhoods and interpolate their decoder behavior for the current image
problem: PEFT requires training loops and labels; but if SAM's failures on a target image are 'known behaviors' elsewhere in embedding space, a retrieval mechanism could borrow correct decoding behavior without any optimization.
core_hypothesis: For moderately shifted domains, target-image embeddings lie near manifolds of generic images where SAM performs well; conditioning the decoder on retrieved neighbor statistics (e.g., shifting the image embedding toward the local manifold, or blending prompt-token embeddings that worked for neighbors) recovers a useful fraction of the adaptation gain at zero training.
falsifiable_prediction: Embedding-shift-by-retrieval will improve zero-shot IoU on moderately-shifted domains by a measurable margin (worst on severe shifts where neighborhoods are empty), and gains will correlate with retrieval density around the target embedding.
why_important: Zero-training adaptation that scales with a public embedding index rather than per-domain labels would serve long-tail users who will never fine-tune, and retrieval density becomes a novel domain-gap meter.
why_possibly_novel: Retrieval-augmentation is established in NLP and image generation; using an embedding index to steer a frozen segmentation decoder, with density-predicted gains, appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build an index of 100k generic-image embeddings; for 3 target domains, apply embedding-shift retrieval conditioning; measure IoU deltas and their correlation with local retrieval density.
main_risk: Embedding arithmetic may break decoder assumptions (embeddings off-manifold after shifting), producing artifacts that erase gains.
default_community_belief: Adaptation means changing parameters; inference-time retrieval cannot substitute for weight updates in dense prediction.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Segmentation quality depends on precise spatial detail unique to each image, which neighborhood statistics cannot supply.
fastest_falsification: Small index, one domain, embedding-shift ablation: two days including index construction.

one_line: SA-1B taught SAM a 'closed-region prior': masks with boundary fractal dimension above a threshold are unrepresentable, predicting exactly which amorphous objects fail
problem: SAM's failures on amorphous, wispy, or porous structures are reported anecdotally per domain, with no unifying quantitative predictor of when an object class will fail regardless of prompting effort.
core_hypothesis: SA-1B masks are overwhelmingly closed regions with low boundary complexity; SAM's decoder inherited this as a structural prior, so per-object failure probability is predicted by boundary fractal dimension (or boundary-length-to-area ratio) with a sharp threshold that is constant across domains.
falsifiable_prediction: Stratifying diverse datasets by mask boundary dimension will reveal a threshold above which zero-shot IoU collapses regardless of contrast and size controls, and the threshold location will be approximately domain-invariant; PEFT will shift performance below the threshold but move the threshold itself only marginally.
why_important: A quantitative representability limit tells practitioners which target classes need architectural or output-representation changes (not tuning), and characterizes the pretraining data's geometric bias precisely.
why_possibly_novel: Failure taxonomies for SAM exist qualitatively; a controlled, dimension-stratified representability study with a domain-invariance claim appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute boundary-complexity statistics for masks across 5 datasets, stratify zero-shot performance controlling for size/contrast, locate thresholds per domain, compare their positions; repeat on one LoRA-tuned model.
main_risk: Boundary dimension correlates with annotation noise (complex boundaries are inconsistently labeled), confounding representability with label quality.
default_community_belief: Amorphous-object failure is a data-coverage problem that domain-specific fine-tuning fixes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The dynamic-filter decoder can express arbitrary per-pixel similarity maps in principle, so the limit may be soft and fully trainable-away.
fastest_falsification: Dimension-stratified zero-shot evaluation across two datasets: pure inference plus statistics, about a day.

one_line: SAM has a 'stuff blindness': unbounded regions (road, water, field) fail not from features but because no prompt type can express 'this material everywhere' — a prompt-language insufficiency result
problem: Adaptation for stuff-like targets (surfaces, materials) uses the same recipes as for objects, and fails oddly; the cause may be that SAM's prompt vocabulary (point/box/mask) cannot specify region-type intent at all.
core_hypothesis: SAM interprets every prompt as indicating a bounded thing; for stuff regions, clicks yield local blobs and boxes yield box-shaped truncations, and this behavior is invariant to feature-level adaptation because the failure is in prompt semantics, provable by showing PEFT on stuff tasks converges to prompt-shape-correlated errors.
falsifiable_prediction: Zero-shot and PEFT-adapted SAM on stuff targets will both show mask-extent statistics strongly correlated with prompt geometry (blob radius around clicks, box-shaped truncation), while a prompt-side extension (multi-click same-material protocol without any weight change) will outperform weight-level PEFT of moderate size.
why_important: It cleanly separates 'model cannot see it' from 'user cannot say it', redirecting stuff-segmentation adaptation toward prompt-protocol design — a cheaper and more portable fix than model surgery.
why_possibly_novel: Things-vs-stuff is an old distinction; formulating it as an expressivity limit of SAM's prompt language, with the prediction that prompt protocols beat weight tuning, appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On stuff-heavy datasets, measure mask-extent-vs-prompt-geometry correlation for zero-shot and adapted models; implement a 3-click same-material prompting protocol on the frozen model and compare against LoRA adaptation.
main_risk: Sufficiently heavy fine-tuning may teach 'click means flood-fill' behavior, contradicting the invariance claim and reducing the result to 'small PEFT is too small'.
default_community_belief: Stuff segmentation failure is a feature/data problem, addressed by fine-tuning on stuff-labeled data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Reported successes of adapted SAM variants on scene-parsing-style tasks suggest prompt semantics may be more malleable than the insufficiency claim assumes.
fastest_falsification: Mask-extent-vs-prompt-geometry statistics on one stuff dataset, zero-shot: hours.

one_line: PEFT fits annotation style, not anatomy: adapters transfer across datasets of the same domain far worse than within annotator styles of different domains — a hidden target-leakage in adaptation research
problem: Adaptation gains are measured on test splits sharing the training set's annotation conventions (boundary tightness, hole handling, occlusion policy), so reported 'domain adaptation' may substantially be annotation-style fitting that fails at deployment against a different labeling pipeline.
core_hypothesis: A significant fraction of measured PEFT gain is attributable to learning label-style parameters (systematic boundary offsets, morphological conventions); style-transfer experiments (same images, relabeled under different conventions) will show adapters transporting poorly across styles, and style-normalizing the labels before training will improve cross-pipeline generalization.
falsifiable_prediction: Cross-style evaluation (train on style 1, test on style 2, same imagery domain) will lose a large share of within-style gains; a simple learned style-normalization (fit a morphological/offset transform between styles on 20 masks) will recover most of that loss.
why_important: It quantifies how much of the field's reported progress is convention-fitting, and provides a cheap corrective (style normalization) that makes adapters portable across institutions — the actual promise of foundation models.
why_possibly_novel: Inter-annotator variation is documented in medical imaging; framing annotation style as a leaky component of PEFT gains, with a decomposition protocol, appears absent from adaptation literature.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Find or create doubly-annotated data (two conventions on the same images); train adapters per style; build the 2x2 transfer matrix; test style-normalization recovery.
main_risk: Truly doubly-annotated sets are scarce; synthetic restyling of labels may not capture real inter-pipeline variation.
default_community_belief: PEFT gains measure domain knowledge acquisition; the test split validates generalization.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Style parameters may be a tiny fraction of the learned signal, with genuine appearance adaptation dominating, making the decomposition an academic footnote.
fastest_falsification: Synthetic restyle (erode/dilate/occlusion-policy change) of one dataset's labels, retrain, cross-evaluate: two GPU-days.

one_line: Everyone trains PEFT with prompts sampled from ground truth, but humans click where errors are salient: saliency-matched prompt simulation changes which adapter wins
problem: Prompt simulation during training and evaluation samples clicks uniformly or at mask centroids; real users click guided by visual saliency and perceived model errors, a distribution mismatch that may silently misrank adaptation methods for deployment.
core_hypothesis: Adapters are ranked differently under GT-uniform prompt simulation versus human-like (saliency- and error-guided) simulation; models tuned under human-like simulation will win human evaluations even when losing standard benchmarks, because prompt distribution is part of the task definition.
falsifiable_prediction: A controlled comparison of adapters trained under the two simulators will show rank inversions on human-in-the-loop evaluation for a meaningful fraction of task pairs, and the human-like-trained adapters will need fewer real-user clicks to target quality.
why_important: If the prompt simulator is a first-order design choice rather than boilerplate, the field needs standardized human-like simulators — this reframes a hidden constant as an experimental variable.
why_possibly_novel: Click-simulation strategies are discussed in interactive segmentation, but their effect on PEFT method ranking for foundation models, verified against real humans, appears unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched adapters under uniform vs saliency/error-guided simulation on 2 tasks; evaluate both with both simulators and with a small real-user study (10 users, clicks-to-target).
main_risk: Human click behavior varies across users and interfaces, so 'human-like' may not be a single distribution, complicating the claim.
default_community_belief: Prompt simulation details are boilerplate that wash out; benchmark rankings transfer to human use.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Adapters may be robust across prompt distributions, making rankings stable and the simulator choice genuinely second-order.
fastest_falsification: Cross-simulator evaluation (no new training) of existing adapters: if rankings are identical across simulators, the premise weakens — one day.

one_line: Oversampling small objects during PEFT backfires beyond a ratio: below the encoder's resolvable size, their gradients are label noise that degrades everything else
problem: Small-object failure prompts practitioners to oversample small instances during adaptation, assuming more signal helps; if many of those instances are below SAM's resolvable size, their supervision is unlearnable and acts as structured noise.
core_hypothesis: Training pressure on sub-resolvable objects cannot be satisfied by any weight configuration reachable via PEFT, so it perturbs shared parameters chaotically; the IoU-vs-oversampling-ratio curve is therefore non-monotone with a peak at moderate ratios, and filtering out sub-resolvable instances beats oversampling them.
falsifiable_prediction: Sweeping small-object oversampling ratios will produce an inverted-U performance curve on both small and large objects, and a size-filtered curriculum (excluding sub-patch objects) will outperform the best oversampling ratio on overall mIoU.
why_important: It corrects a widespread and intuitive-but-wrong data practice, connects to the resolvability limit (making it actionable), and provides a data-curation rule any team can apply immediately.
why_possibly_novel: Class rebalancing lore is generic; identifying an architectural resolvability threshold as the mechanism that turns oversampling into noise, for promptable segmenters, appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One dataset with size-stratified labels: sweep oversampling ratios {1,2,4,8,16}x for objects under 2 patches, plot overall and per-stratum IoU, then test the filtered curriculum.
main_risk: The inverted-U may be shallow at practical ratios, making the correction real but low-stakes.
default_community_belief: Oversampling hard/rare cases is a safe, standard remedy for class imbalance in fine-tuning.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Even sub-resolvable objects may provide usable gradient signal via context learning (predicting from surroundings), making their supervision partially learnable.
fastest_falsification: Three oversampling ratios on one dataset: two GPU-days to see whether the curve bends down.

one_line: The embedding-cache shortcut defines a measurable 'decoder-only ceiling': map which task families PEFT can solve with 1000x cheaper cached-embedding training
problem: If only decoder-side parameters are tuned, image embeddings can be precomputed once, making training absurdly cheap; but nobody has mapped when this restriction is harmless versus crippling, so practitioners either overpay (full pipelines) or get silently capped.
core_hypothesis: Task families partition by whether their domain gap is decodable from frozen embeddings: label-convention shifts, granularity shifts, and mild photometric shifts hit the decoder-only ceiling near full-PEFT performance, while modality and texture-statistics shifts fall far below it, and the partition is predictable from a frozen-feature probe.
falsifiable_prediction: Across >=8 tasks, decoder-only (cached) PEFT will reach >90% of full-PEFT gains on the first three shift families and <50% on the latter two, with a probe-based classifier predicting family membership beforehand at high accuracy.
why_important: A validated 'ceiling map' would let most practitioners adapt SAM on a laptop with cached embeddings, democratizing adaptation and reserving GPU-heavy encoder tuning for tasks that provably need it.
why_possibly_novel: Decoder-only tuning is common as a convenience choice; the systematic ceiling measurement across shift taxonomies, with a pre-hoc predictor, appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble 8 tasks spanning the hypothesized families, run decoder-only vs full-LoRA at matched data, compute ceiling fractions, then validate the probe predictor.
main_risk: The shift-family taxonomy may be too leaky (real tasks mix families), blurring the clean partition into a continuum.
default_community_belief: Encoder adaptation is generally necessary for real domain gaps; decoder-only tuning is a toy shortcut.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Frozen embeddings may carry far more OOD information than assumed, making the ceiling near-universal and the map boring (or the reverse).
fastest_falsification: Two contrasting tasks (label-shift vs modality-shift), both regimes: two GPU-days for the first partition evidence.

one_line: Refinement clicks don't need the full encoder: cached mid-layer features suffice for click updates, enabling early-exit interactive SAM
problem: Interactive latency is dominated by the encoder, which current systems run once and cache; but adaptation scenarios that tune the encoder break the cache, and nobody knows how much encoder depth click-refinement actually consumes.
core_hypothesis: The information needed to respond to corrective clicks is present in mid-depth features (later blocks mostly refine semantics, not the local evidence corrections rely on); an early-exit pathway (shallow features + decoder) can process refinement clicks with minimal quality loss, reserving full depth for the first prediction only.
falsifiable_prediction: Feeding block-k features (k at half depth) through a lightly-tuned neck for refinement-only passes will preserve >95% of the final click-curve quality while cutting refinement latency several-fold, and the required k will be lower for corrective clicks than for initial prompts.
why_important: It changes the latency architecture of interactive segmentation (first click slow, corrections instant) and reveals which computation depth interactivity actually uses — a scientific and an engineering payoff.
why_possibly_novel: Early-exit research targets classification confidence; depth-requirements of interactive correction in promptable segmenters appear unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Extract features at 4 depths, train tiny bridging necks per depth (decoder frozen), evaluate click curves using full-depth first pass plus early-exit refinements across 2 datasets.
main_risk: Mid-layer features may lack the global disambiguation needed when a correction flips the object hypothesis entirely.
default_community_belief: All prompts need the same full-quality embedding; the encoder is a monolithic prerequisite.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Corrections that change object identity (not just boundary) plausibly need exactly the deep semantics early exits discard.
fastest_falsification: Zero-training probe: run refinement with truncated-depth embeddings through the existing neck (accepting mismatch) to bound the effect — hours.

one_line: Interactivity is the hard-to-distill component: students distilled from adapted SAM inherit single-shot accuracy but lose the correction loop, and nobody measures it
problem: Distillation of adapted SAM into small deployable students is standard practice, validated on single-shot mIoU; if interactive refinement behavior does not transfer through standard distillation losses, deployed students are silently worse products.
core_hypothesis: Click-response behavior is a conditional function (output given prompt-history) that pointwise mask-matching losses do not constrain off the teacher's greedy trajectory; students therefore match first-click outputs but diverge on correction dynamics, requiring trajectory-level distillation (matching behavior across simulated interaction rollouts) to inherit interactivity.
falsifiable_prediction: Standard-distilled students will show markedly flatter click curves than teachers at matched first-click IoU, and rollout-based distillation will close most of that interactivity gap at equal student capacity.
why_important: The result would establish interactive fidelity as a first-class distillation objective and explain field reports of small SAM variants feeling 'stubborn' under correction despite good benchmarks.
why_possibly_novel: Distillation for segmentation matches masks or features; distilling the interaction policy dimension of promptable models appears unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Distill one adapted teacher into a small student with standard losses; evaluate click curves for both; implement rollout distillation (match outputs along simulated click sequences) and re-evaluate.
main_risk: Rollout distillation multiplies training cost; if the interactivity gap turns out small, the fix costs more than the problem.
default_community_belief: Matching masks and features transfers the model; interactivity follows automatically from output fidelity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If student architectures share the dense-prompt feedback design, correction behavior may transfer through ordinary losses better than hypothesized.
fastest_falsification: Click-curve comparison of any existing distilled SAM variant against its teacher: pure evaluation, one day.

one_line: Oracle-prompt evaluation inflates and reorders PEFT method rankings: the field's league tables may not survive realistic prompting
problem: Adaptation papers evaluate with idealized prompts (GT-derived tight boxes, center clicks); deployment sees noisy detector boxes and human clicks, and if method rankings are prompt-protocol-dependent, the literature's comparative claims are unreliable guides.
core_hypothesis: PEFT methods differ in prompt-noise robustness (some overfit to clean-prompt structure), so switching from oracle to realistic prompt protocols changes not just absolute numbers but the ordering of methods, at a rate high enough to matter for method selection.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-evaluating >=5 published-style PEFT variants under noisy-box and human-like-click protocols will invert at least some pairwise rankings that were significant under oracle prompts, and the inversion probability will grow with prompt-noise level.
why_important: Evaluation protocol is the field's coordination mechanism; demonstrating protocol-dependent rankings would force reporting standards (both protocols, always) and change which methods practitioners copy.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt-robustness is acknowledged qualitatively; a systematic ranking-stability study across prompt protocols for adaptation methods appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Five adaptation variants on 2 datasets, evaluated under oracle, noisy-box (calibrated detector-like noise), and simulated-human-click protocols; compute ranking stability statistics.
main_risk: If all methods degrade proportionally, rankings are stable and the result is a (still useful) null.
default_community_belief: Oracle-prompt benchmarks are a fair comparative basis; noise affects all methods equally.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Prompt noise may be a second-order perturbation relative to method differences, leaving orderings intact.
fastest_falsification: Two methods, two protocols, one dataset: a day with cached checkpoints; a stable ranking across protocols undermines the strong claim early.

one_line: Two adapters with equal mIoU can differ 2x in prompt-sensitivity variance: report variance-over-prompts as a first-class metric or ship lotteries
problem: Mean IoU over a fixed prompt protocol is the universal adaptation metric; it hides how much output quality varies when the same object is prompted slightly differently, which is what users actually experience as reliability.
core_hypothesis: Adaptation methods differ systematically in the variance of quality across equivalent prompts (some fit narrow prompt-conditional solutions), and this variance dimension is uncorrelated enough with mean IoU that model selection by mean alone regularly picks the less deployable model.
falsifiable_prediction: Across adapter pairs matched on mean IoU (within 0.5 points), prompt-sensitivity variance will differ by a factor >=1.5 in a substantial fraction of pairs, and human raters will prefer the low-variance model at matched means.
why_important: Adding a cheap second axis (variance over a standardized prompt-perturbation set) to standard evaluation would realign research incentives with deployment reliability at almost no cost.
why_possibly_novel: Robustness metrics exist for input corruptions; a standardized prompt-perturbation variance metric for adapted promptable models, validated against user preference, appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For 6 adapters across 3 tasks, compute mean and variance under a fixed prompt-jitter battery; find matched-mean pairs; run a small preference study on the divergent pairs.
main_risk: Variance may correlate strongly with mean after all (better models are also more stable), collapsing the second axis into the first.
default_community_belief: Mean IoU under a fixed protocol adequately summarizes adapter quality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For most practical adapters the variance differences may be small enough that the metric adds noise, not signal.
fastest_falsification: Variance battery over existing checkpoints: pure inference, one day; strong mean-variance correlation kills the case.

one_line: 'SAM fails on X' papers under-tune the baseline: oracle selection among SAM's three masks plus threshold calibration closes a large share of claimed domain gaps
problem: Dozens of adaptation papers motivate themselves by SAM's poor zero-shot numbers on their domain, typically computed with default mask selection and thresholds; the honest zero-shot ceiling (best of three masks, calibrated threshold, best prompt placement) is rarely reported, possibly inflating the field's perceived progress.
core_hypothesis: A standardized 'strong zero-shot' protocol will close a substantial fraction (hypothesized 30-60%) of reported gaps across published task setups, meaning much of what adaptation papers claim as learned domain knowledge is recoverable by evaluation hygiene alone.
falsifiable_prediction: Recomputing zero-shot baselines on >=6 domains with oracle-of-3 selection, per-domain threshold calibration (from 10 labeled masks), and prompt-placement optimization will reduce the zero-shot-to-finetuned gap by the hypothesized fraction, and some published relative improvements will fall within the recovered margin.
why_important: Cheap corrections to baseline practice recalibrate the field's understanding of how much adaptation is actually needed, and give practitioners an immediately deployable 'tuning-free first resort'.
why_possibly_novel: Individual tricks are known; the systematic audit quantifying how much claimed adaptation gain is baseline slack, across multiple domains, appears not to exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Six diverse domains with public zero-shot claims or reproducible setups: compute default vs strong zero-shot vs a standard LoRA fine-tune; report gap decompositions.
main_risk: Oracle-of-3 selection uses ground truth and must be carefully framed (as a ceiling, with a learned selector as the honest variant) to avoid overclaiming.
default_community_belief: Reported zero-shot numbers reflect SAM's real capability floor on a domain; gaps to fine-tuned models measure needed adaptation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: On genuinely hard domains all three masks may be bad and thresholds irrelevant, leaving gaps untouched and the audit result unremarkable.
fastest_falsification: One domain, default vs strong zero-shot protocol: a few hours; a negligible difference on the first hard domain deflates the hypothesis.

one_line: Attention-bias PEFT: adapt SAM by learning additive attention-logit biases (relative-position deltas) instead of weight deltas — geometry-targeted adaptation at ~0.001% parameters
problem: LoRA modifies what features are computed, but some domain shifts are primarily geometric (different object scales, elongations, spatial layouts); adapting feature weights to fix geometry is indirect and parameter-wasteful.
core_hypothesis: Adding small learned biases to attention logits (per-head, as a function of relative position) directly retunes the spatial mixing kernel of each attention layer; for geometry-dominated shifts this matches LoRA quality with orders of magnitude fewer parameters and greater interpretability (the learned biases show what geometry changed).
falsifiable_prediction: On scale- and layout-shifted tasks, attention-bias tuning will match rank-4 LoRA within 1 IoU point at <1% of its parameters, while on texture/modality shifts it will clearly lose; visualized bias fields will correlate with the known geometric transformation of the domain.
why_important: A geometry-specific adaptation channel completes a taxonomy (content adapters vs geometry adapters), enables extreme parameter efficiency, and produces human-readable evidence of what the domain shift was.
why_possibly_novel: Relative-position bias tuning exists as an architecture feature; isolating it as the sole adaptation mechanism for promptable segmentation, with the geometry-vs-content specialization claim, appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Two geometric shifts (aerial scale, elongated industrial objects) and two content shifts; attention-bias vs LoRA at matched data; visualize and interpret learned biases.
main_risk: SAM's attention implementation may not expose a clean relative-position parameterization, requiring approximations that dilute the mechanism.
default_community_belief: Weight-space adapters (LoRA and kin) are the universal PEFT mechanism; attention logits are not an adaptation surface.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Geometric shifts may be entangled with content shifts in all real domains, denying the mechanism a regime where it wins cleanly.
fastest_falsification: One synthetic pure-scale shift, bias-tuning vs LoRA: one to two GPU-days.

one_line: Background-token pruning during adaptation is a regularizer: dropping low-relevance tokens from global attention improves OOD boundary precision by removing background interference
problem: Token pruning is studied purely as an efficiency trick with quality treated as a cost to minimize; for domain adaptation, background tokens carrying OOD statistics may actively harm foreground decoding, making pruning a quality intervention.
core_hypothesis: Out-of-domain backgrounds inject unfamiliar key/value content into global attention, perturbing foreground token refinement; pruning (or downweighting) tokens with low prompt-relevance during adapted inference reduces this interference, improving boundary metrics specifically in cluttered OOD scenes.
falsifiable_prediction: Prompt-conditioned token pruning at moderate ratios will improve OOD boundary-F over the unpruned adapted model (not merely match it) in high-clutter scenes, with gains vanishing in-domain and in low-clutter scenes — an interaction that the efficiency framing cannot explain.
why_important: Reframing pruning as regularization gives a free quality knob for OOD deployment and evidence about how background context helps or hurts foundation segmenters outside their training distribution.
why_possibly_novel: Pruning-for-quality (not speed) with a clutter-conditional prediction, in the adaptation setting, appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On 2 OOD datasets stratified by clutter (background object density), sweep pruning ratios with prompt-distance-based token scoring; measure boundary-F and region IoU per stratum, in-domain controls included.
main_risk: Aggressive pruning may remove genuinely needed context (e.g., disambiguating similar adjacent objects), causing losses that mask the interference effect.
default_community_belief: More context never hurts; token reduction trades quality for speed by definition.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Attention may already learn to ignore irrelevant OOD background via low attention weights, leaving nothing for pruning to fix.
fastest_falsification: Inference-only pruning sweep on one cluttered OOD set: hours, no training.

one_line: A tiny frequency-domain adapter branch (FFT features injected at the neck) rescues domains where SAM's spatial features are blind, e.g., low-contrast periodic textures
problem: Some target structures (subtle texture boundaries, periodic materials) are nearly invisible in SAM's spatial feature maps, and spatial-domain adapters can only reweight what the frozen encoder computed; information genuinely absent from the embedding cannot be recovered by any LoRA.
core_hypothesis: A small parallel branch computing spectral features of local patches and injecting them additively at the neck supplies exactly the class of information (narrowband texture statistics) that the frozen encoder discards, complementing rather than duplicating spatial features; its gains will concentrate on texture-defined boundaries and be near-zero elsewhere.
falsifiable_prediction: On texture-boundary-heavy tasks the spectral branch will beat parameter-matched spatial adapters (extra LoRA rank) decisively, while on photometric-boundary tasks the two will tie — a double dissociation identifying what the encoder lacks.
why_important: It tests a general principle for foundation-model adaptation: when the pretrained representation provably lacks a feature class, inject it at the narrowest interface instead of fine-tuning deeper — a pattern reusable beyond SAM.
why_possibly_novel: Frequency-domain side-inputs exist in low-level vision; using them as a targeted representational patch for a frozen segmentation foundation model, with the dissociation-based validation, appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Two texture-boundary datasets and two photometric-boundary controls; spectral branch vs extra-rank LoRA at matched parameters; per-boundary-type error analysis.
main_risk: The neck may be an information bottleneck that clips injected features unless the decoder is also lightly tuned, complicating the parameter-matched comparison.
default_community_belief: The pretrained encoder computes sufficient features; adaptation is about reweighting, not injecting new signal families.
why_it_might_be_wrong: ViT encoders may retain more texture-spectral information than assumed, making the injection redundant and the dissociation absent.
fastest_falsification: Linear-probe check first: can texture boundaries be decoded from frozen embeddings at all? Hours; if yes, the premise of missing information collapses.

one_line: The 'optical adapter': a single tuned 3x3 input convolution (dozens of parameters) matches encoder LoRA on intensity-remapped domains — the domain gap is at the sensor, fix it at the sensor
problem: For modality shifts that are approximately pointwise intensity transforms (different sensors, stains, exposure regimes), the community reflexively adapts deep layers, using thousands of times more parameters than the underlying transformation needs.
core_hypothesis: When the domain map is approximately a local pixel-space transformation, the minimal sufficient adapter is an input-space convolution that inverts it; a tuned 3x3 conv (possibly per-channel affine plus one nonlinearity) will match encoder LoRA on such domains and its failure signals that the shift is genuinely feature-level — a built-in diagnostic.
